2da15531c18fbccf: PORT DICKSON, Oct 22 — A final-year college student undergoing practical training at a hotel in Lukut was found dead behind an eatery here yesterday.
Port Dickson District Police Chief Supt Ahmad Afiq Mohd Adnan said the 21-year-old man was found at 6.05 am after police received an emergency call via the MERS 999 line from a member of the public.
He said preliminary investigations found that the victim had facial injuries and a broken arm, believed to have been sustained in a fall from a building.
“The post-mortem found that the cause of death was head and abdominal injuries resulting from a fall from a height.
“Investigations also found no criminal elements in the case,” he said in a statement yesterday.
Ahmad Afiq said the victim was believed to have been staying in a rented room in a three-storey building used as a hostel near where the body was found.
An inspection of the room found no signs of a break-in, and no valuables or personal documents were missing.
The victim’s body was taken to Port Dickson Hospital, and the case has been classified as sudden death (SDR).
Members of the public with information about the incident are urged to assist with the investigation.
They are also advised against speculation out of respect for the victim’s family. — Bernama

6e26b6f581c16928: SINGAPORE, Oct 22 — Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Ltd (OCBC) yesterday announced the addition of Malaysian ringgit (MYR) to its multi-currency savings accounts beginning October 23, 2026, making it the first non-Malaysian bank to enable customers to hold the currency in a Singapore-based personal savings account.

In a statement, the bank said customers can convert Singapore dollars into MYR at competitive exchange rates without any hidden fees or high mark-ups through their OCBC Global Savings Account and Premier Global Savings Account.
They can hold up to RM50,000 and subsequently earn interest on their ringgit cash balances.
“As MYR is a tightly controlled non-internationalised currency, opportunities for individuals to hold the currency in bank accounts outside Malaysia are limited.
“The addition of MYR now further strengthens OCBC’s multi-currency savings account, which allows customers to hold and manage 11 currencies within a single account,” it said on Wednesday.

According to OCBC, Malaysia is its customers’ most popular overseas spending destination, accounting for one in three overseas transactions, with dining and shopping as the two largest spending categories.
The upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link is expected to further drive cross-border travel and consumer spending across the causeway, it added.

OCBC head of group wealth management, Tan Siew Lee said the launch of ringgit on OCBC’s Global Savings Account will be particularly powerful for many Singaporeans who make frequent cross-border trips to Malaysia.

“It gives them the ability to lock in favourable exchange rates ahead of time, hold ringgit in a regulated Singapore deposit account, earn interest on cash balances, protect against future currency swings, and enjoy greater certainty over their travel spending.
“This means that they no longer have to choose between favourable exchange rates and growing their savings. Instead, they can now do both,” she said. — Bernama
208ed8a99918f170: WASHINGTON, Oct 22 — The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Wednesday, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a social media post explaining the measure.
“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority,” he added.

A diplomatic source in the Middle East told AFP that some families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, but Pigott stressed that Wednesday’s order was for the departure of non-emergency embassy staff and their families in Saudi Arabia only.

Saudi Arabia has this month come under near-daily attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the kingdom’s deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.
On Wednesday, the Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured a further two.
“The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others,” the ministry said in a statement.
It did not say who launched the drone aimed at Shaybah oil field near the UAE border. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported intercepting six drones.
One person was killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, aviation officials said.
In June, a four-year-old truce in Yemen’s civil war collapsed, reviving the conflict that dates back to 2014. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the internationally recognised government since 2015.

The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February and again in July before US President Donald Trump called off a new wave of strikes.
Late on Wednesday, Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a spell of relative calm.
“A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province,” the official IRNA news agency said.
It added that “local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions.”
In late February, the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, killing the country’s supreme leader, along with senior military commanders.
Iran has attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, demanding all ships seek its authorisation to cross. In peacetime, the strategic waterway carried around a fifth of the world’s oil supplies.
In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships. — AFP
b4ee8219e42e74e3: KUALA LUMPUR: A total of 13,072 doctor posts in the Health Ministry were vacant as of June 30, Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said.
Of the vacancies, 1,660 were for specialist medical officers, while the remaining 11,412 were for non-specialist medical officers.
Meanwhile, Dzulkefly said the Health Ministry recorded 3,510 resignations among permanent and contract medical officers between 2024 and 2026.
Of the total, 1,252 were permanent medical officers, while the remaining 2,258 were contract medical officers.
He said the ministry also recorded eight medical specialists who resigned or migrated overseas.
He added the resignations were out of a total of 14,064 medical officers appointed on a permanent basis and 9,847 on a contract basis by the ministry during the period.
Based on ministry records, Dzulkefly said the main reason for resignations was employment in the private sector, accounting for 51.4 per cent of cases.

"Personal reasons accounted for 36.8 per cent, followed by service with statutory bodies (4.5 per cent), working or residing overseas (2.9 per cent), health problems (2.6 per cent), furthering studies (1.5 per cent) and opening their own clinics (0.3 per cent)," he said in a written parliamentary reply to a question from V Ganabatirau (PH-Klang).

Ganabatirau had sought information on doctors resigning or migrating overseas, vacancies, specialist shortages, waiting times for housemanship placements and the effectiveness of measures to retain doctors.
Among the immediate measures to address the issue, he said a task force established by the Public Service Department in April was examining staffing issues.
"The ministry had also been given greater authority to manage and distribute approved positions to expedite recruitment."

In a separate development, Dzulkefly said six government hospitals had met the target of treating at least 70 per cent of non-emergency patients within two hours, compared with previous average waiting times of between four and six hours.

In a reply to Datuk Dr Zulkafperi Hanapi (Ind-Tanjong Karang), he said Raja Permaisuri Bainun Hospital in Ipoh recorded the highest performance, with 98.61 per cent of patients in the green zone receiving treatment within the two-hour target.

Ampang Hospital ranked second at 88.78 per cent, followed by Selayang Hospital at 74.1 per cent, Sultanah Aminah Hospital in Johor Baru at 73.2 per cent, Tengku Ampuan Rahimah Hospital in Klang at 72.2 per cent and Kuala Lumpur Hospital at 71.8 per cent.
"Patient attendance at the six major hospitals also fell by nine per cent after selected government health clinics extended their operating hours," Dzulkefly said.
He said the clinics now operate until 9pm on weekdays and from 8am to 1pm on weekends and public holidays.
"This measure to divert minor cases to health clinics has demonstrated an immediate impact, recording a reduction in physical patient attendance," he said.
28999b730a1c5f73: NEW YORK, Oct 22 — Tesla reported lower third-quarter profits Wednesday as near-trillionaire Elon Musk’s electric vehicle maker ramped up huge investments in artificial intelligence and other envelope-pushing technologies.

Besides marginally lower car sales, Tesla saw a drop in revenues from regulatory credits and energy and storage, while spending on research and development more than doubled as the company engages in a spending binge on AI, robotics and autonomous transport.

The earnings arguably upstaged Musk’s disclosure Tuesday that special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to discuss a merger of the two companies. Musk, who leads both companies, declined to offer further details Wednesday.

The potential merger — which some have dubbed “Elon Inc” — boosted shares of both companies on Wednesday, lifting Musk’s wealth back near US$1 trillion (RM4.08 trillion) at US$989 billion, according to Forbes’ real-time billionaires index.
In the third quarter, Tesla reported profits of US$787 million, down 42.7 per cent from the year-ago period. Revenues were essentially flat at US$28 billion.
Analysts had been cautious about Tesla’s latest results heading into Wednesday’s release.
While third-quarter auto sales topped estimates, due in part to an uptick in European markets amid high gasoline prices, better sales have not always translated to Tesla’s bottom line.
The company has faced questions about the rollout of Tesla’s robotaxi venture that has progressed much more slowly than hoped.
Musk has repeatedly made overly rosy forecasts about self-driving technology, as in 2019 when predicted there would be more than a million robotaxis the following year.
In Texas, where Tesla has focused its robotaxi launch, there are currently about 800 robotaxis, according to FSD Database.
Tesla’s release highlighted the September 3 launch of robotaxi service in Austin and said “cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles grew eightfold quarter over quarter.”

Company officials said Wednesday that if the current pace of robotaxi growth continues, the venture could be meaningful financially as early as next year. The ramp-up is guided by a strong desire to avoid safety problems, company officials said.

For much of this year, Tesla has also encountered scrutiny over a steep increase in annual capital spending to US$25 billion or more to fund ambitious programs in artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous driving.
Capital spending more than doubled in the third quarter to US$4.7 billion, although that was below the US$7.8 billion expected by Wall Street analysts.
Besides robotaxi and AI, Tesla is heavily investing in Musk’s “Optimus” humanoid robots as well as the buildout jointly with SpaceX of a large chip factory in Austin.
The chip factory, called Terafab, was the object of some of Musk’s most effusive and self-boosting language on Wednesday.
“Terafab I think will be the most valuable building in the world, and and will probably have an economic value that will place it in the top 20 of countries,” he said.
Musk is also eyeing auto growth, projecting production of five million in 2030 compared with 1.7 million in 2025.
“After many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we’re now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth,” Musk said.
Looming SpaceX merger?
But questions about Tesla’s future loomed larger with talk of the potential SpaceX tie-up. The companies have a combined equity value of more than US$3.5 trillion.
“We think it’s a matter of when, not if” the two companies combine, said CFRA Research equity analyst Garrett Nelson.
“That’s the whole issue,” Nelson said of a potential mega-deal. “Tesla as we know it today may not exist in six to 12 months.”
On SpaceX’s conference call Tuesday night, Musk said the committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will.
Musk said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.

Talk of the deal heaps additional attention on Musk as the billionaire’s latest cash infusion into US political elections fuels fresh criticism. Musk has steered at least US$276 million to allies of President Donald Trump in the Republican party.

Musk is also under scrutiny over a report he ordered a reduction in Starshield telecom services for Ukraine, adding to pressure on the country at the same time Trump has criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and called for him to be replaced.
Shares of Tesla initially rose in after-hours trading, but were down 2.8 per cent near 2250 GMT. — AFP
bafdbff54c09f400: KUCHING, Oct 22 — Tunku Putra-HELP (TPH) International School has confirmed that it will immediately enhance its campus security measures, including stationing three ancillary police officers on its grounds, following an incident where a teacher was injured by a student yesterday.

The school management announced that safety checks will be conducted upon entry to the campus with immediate effect, as part of a broader review to implement long-term security measures in consultation with relevant authorities.
“While existing safety measures remain in place, TPH has reviewed its safety protocols and has enhanced security measures in consultation with the relevant authorities.
“The school is also exploring more comprehensive, long-term security measures for the campus.

“The Senior Leadership Team will hold assemblies for students to address the incident, provide assurance, respond appropriately to their concerns and provide counselling support for those who may need it,” the school posted on its official Facebook account yesterday.

TPH also confirmed that the school will resume classes tomorrow after receiving clearance from all relevant authorities, following an early closure today as a precautionary measure advised by the police.
Providing an update on the victim, the school stated that the injured teacher was taken to the hospital by ambulance and is currently recovering well with no critical injuries.
It clarified that the alleged student is in police custody and is no longer an active student of TPH, while urging the public not to circulate unverified information or speculate on the incident.
Earlier, Acting Sarawak Police Commissioner DCP Saifullizan Ishak confirmed the male Form Four student’s arrest and revealed that police seized a penknife and a small axe in connection with the case.

He added that the student has been released on police bail and the case is being investigated under Section 324 of the Penal Code for causing hurt with dangerous weapons, as well as Section 6(1) of the Explosives Act 1957. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: DCP stands for Deputy Commissioner of Police.

Pang Ron-Pei Jing prevailed against China’s Gao Jia Xuan-Wu Meng Ying 14-21, 21-15, 21-15 in 46 minutes to set up a meeting with Taiwan’s Liu Kuang Heng-Hsu Yin-Hui, who stunned fifth seeds from Thailand Dechapol Puavaranukroh-Supissara Paewsampran 21-13, 22-24, 22-20.

3f932efb8d50cfd6: ISTANBUL, Oct 22 — One person was killed and eight others injured in an attack late Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, the country’s civil aviation authority said, Anadolu Ajansi reported.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the injured were immediately taken to the hospital for treatment, with their conditions ranging from minor to severe.
The attack also caused material damage that authorities were still assessing, it added, saying further updates would follow.
The authority did not specify the nature of the attack.

Earlier Wednesday, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said two people were killed and two others injured by falling debris after air defences intercepted a drone targeting an Aramco facility at the Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province.
The debris cause a fire in a contractor’s vehicle, but operations at the oil field were unaffected, according to the ministry.
The Saudi-led coalition also announced Wednesday that it intercepted and destroyed five drones launched toward the kingdom, including in the Eastern Province and Medina region.
King Fahd International Airport previously came under attack on October 11, prompting damage assessments and safety inspections.
The incidents came amid escalating hostilities between Yemen’s Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition, including attacks targeting Saudi airports and energy facilities. — Bernama-Anadolu

958cccde04fe3608: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is targeting RM305 billion in green investments by 2030, with a stronger emphasis on ensuring local companies capture a bigger share of the opportunities through higher-value contracts, technology transfer and skilled job creation.

Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) deputy chief executive officer (Investment Development) Zuaida Abdullah said Malaysia had recorded RM45.8 billion in green investments to date, including RM12.5 billion in the renewable energy (RE) sector.

Between 2023 and 2025, MIDA approved nearly RM10 billion in renewable energy investments spanning solar, mini-hydro and bioenergy projects, underscoring the country's efforts to expand its clean energy capacity.
Investment momentum remained strong in the first half of 2026, with Malaysia approving RM218.5 billion in investments expected to generate more than 99,000 jobs.

However, Zuaida said attracting capital alone was insufficient, with the broader priority being to ensure investments generate lasting economic benefits by strengthening domestic supply chains, developing local expertise and creating quality employment.

She said MIDA was shifting towards an outcome-based approach to investment promotion, particularly through the new manufacturing sector incentive framework, which rewards companies for developing local suppliers, facilitating technology transfer and creating quality jobs.

The approach is intended to ensure foreign and domestic investments contribute more meaningfully to Malaysia's industrial capabilities rather than merely adding to headline investment figures, she told Bernama in an exclusive interview.

Olive Tree Property Consultants chief executive officer Samuel Tan said Malaysia's ability to translate its green investment ambitions into tangible economic gains would depend on how effectively local businesses were integrated into the renewable energy supply chain.

He told Business Times that greater domestic participation would help Malaysian companies build technical expertise, secure higher-value contracts and capture a larger share of the economic benefits as demand for green technologies and infrastructure expanded.
At the Greentech & Eco Products Exhibition & Conference Malaysia (IGEM) 2026, held from Oct 7 to 9, MIDA targeted RM4 billion in potential investments in the renewable energy sector.
Zuaida said Malaysia needed to prioritise domestic companies and local talent as demand for RE infrastructure expanded, supported by stable policies, reliable suppliers and a skilled workforce.

Major project owners, including TNB Power Generation Sdn Bhd and TNB Renewables Sdn Bhd, play a strategic role in driving project development, while engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) contractors coordinate procurement, installation and testing.

These contractors also help identify qualified local vendors for components such as solar photovoltaic modules, inverters, mounting structures and cables, creating opportunities for Malaysian suppliers to participate in the renewable energy value chain.

Zuaida said that MIDA was actively working to connect local companies with major project developers by assisting domestic businesses in meeting the necessary technical standards and qualification requirements to secure contracts.

The initiative is particularly relevant to the sixth cycle of the Large-Scale Solar (LSS6) programme, which incorporates battery energy storage systems (BESS) with a total capacity of 2,650 megawatts.

Under the Energy Transition and Water Transformation Ministry's policy, bidders using locally manufactured solar photovoltaic modules are given priority during the competitive evaluation process, providing an avenue for domestic manufacturers to strengthen their position in the growing clean energy market.
The government's latest green energy initiatives under Budget 2027 are expected to further expand investment opportunities across the sector.
MIDA welcomed the measures announced by Prime Minister and Finance Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, including a RM1.5 billion investment to install solar systems at government buildings.
A dedicated 150-megawatt allocation under LSS6 has also been reserved for Bumiputera companies, supporting broader participation in the green economy.

Meanwhile, Tenaga Nasional Bhd plans to invest RM15 billion to strengthen the national electricity grid, while UEM Lestra is planning a RM1 billion energy storage system project at Kuala Lumpur International Airport.
UEM Lestra is also planning a one-gigawatt hybrid energy project in Johor, adding to the pipeline of large-scale renewable energy developments.
MIDA also welcomed the RM1 billion Climate Fund announced by Kumpulan Wang Persaraan (Diperbadankan) (KWAP), which will be dedicated entirely to green projects.
On the incentives front, the government has extended and enhanced the Green Investment Tax Allowance (GITA), offering investment tax allowances of up to 100 per cent until Dec 31, 2030.
The incentive is aimed at accelerating investment in renewable energy, decarbonisation and green technologies by encouraging businesses to adopt cleaner and more sustainable practices.

Tan said consistent policy support, effective investment incentives and continued infrastructure development would be important in sustaining Malaysia's green investment momentum and enabling local companies to participate more competitively in the transition.

Ultimately, he said the success of the country's green investment drive should be measured not only by the amount of capital attracted, but also by its ability to develop competitive Malaysian businesses, strengthen domestic industrial capabilities and retain more economic value within the country.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
c0992ac890725df6: IPOH: Employment opportunities have overtaken the cost of living as the main concern among Perak residents, according to a survey by Institut Darul Ridzuan (IDR).
The shift in public priorities could reflect changing expectations of the state government's efforts to improve livelihoods under the Perak Sejahtera 2030 development agenda.
IDR chief executive officer Dr Zulqarnain Mohamad said the previous year's survey had identified cost of living as the main concern among respondents.
He said the latest findings suggested that residents were now placing greater emphasis on employment opportunities.
"Last year, the main concern was the cost of living. However, I believe the state government has introduced various initiatives, including Pasar Sejahtera Rakyat, which have helped the people.
"These efforts appear to have had a positive impact, with residents recognising the state government's initiatives.
"The survey also found that 66.4 per cent of respondents considered their monthly income sufficient, while 58.7 per cent said they could set aside money for emergency savings," he said.

He told reporters this after organising a dinner with Perak media practitioner at a hotel here last night. Also present was Perak Association of Media Practitioners president Sayed Mohd Hesham Syed Idris.
Zulqarnain said the findings were encouraging, although the survey did not establish the actual amount respondents had saved.
"We did not ask respondents about the exact amount of their emergency savings, so we cannot determine how much they had put aside," he said.
He said the survey also assessed residents' psychological capital, which measured their confidence and outlook for the future.
"The index recorded a score of 3.9 out of five, equivalent to 78 per cent," he added.
He said the findings indicated that residents were confident the state government could help improve their standard of living and overall well-being.
"Public confidence is important as it motivates us to work harder to improve the standard of living and socio-economic well-being of the people of Perak.
"However, we must continue working hard to ensure that this confidence translates into tangible improvements," he said.
IDR is an independent, non-profit think tank devoted to socio-economic research and development for the state government.
Meanwhile, he said IDR will hold its Perak Economic Outlook programme on Nov 16 to discuss the state's economic ecosystem, future direction and strategies to attract investment.
Zulqarnain said the programme would be among the institute's major initiatives this year.
"IDR will also hold its third Intellectual Discourse session of the year, focusing on ageing in Perak, which has one of the country's highest proportions of senior citizens," he added.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

bba046a2ca8779aa: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — The Ministry of Education (MOE) plans to strengthen the competencies of mathematics teachers through targeted training and the strategic placement of qualified mathematics teachers.
This initiative aims to enhance students’ mastery of the subject and their ability to apply mathematics in daily life.

Deputy director of the Science and Mathematics Sector at MOE’s Curriculum Development Division Dr Aszunarni Ayob said that the Mathematics Teacher Competency Standards – developed under the Malaysia Mathematics Education Transformation Plan (RTPMM) 2026-2035 – will allow for training programmes to be tailored to the specific needs and competency levels of individual teachers.
“Through these standards, we will be able to gauge the competency levels of our teachers, which will then allow us to provide them with targeted training.

“We will not implement a ‘one-size-fits-all’ training programme for all teachers,” she said while as a guest on the Bernama TV programme Ruang Bicara entitled “RTPMM 2026-2035: Nurturing a Mathematically Literate Generation,” here last evening.
She said teachers with expertise in the field will be appointed as ‘Mathematics Specialists’ to mentor their peers.
Furthermore, several Teacher Education Institutes (IPG) will be designated as centres for mathematics education, focusing on teacher training in this specific domain.
Aszunarni said the deployment of teachers specialising in mathematics is being coordinated to ensure their expertise is utilised optimally.

This aligns with the six core pillars of the RTPMM, which encompass governance, curriculum and assessment, teacher competency, co-curricular activities and support, infrastructure, and collaborative networks.
She explained that the understanding of mathematical concepts will be strengthened under the 2027 School Curriculum (KP2027) through a Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract approach.
Meanwhile, the ‘Bilik Darjah Fikrah’ approach encourages students to articulate their problem-solving processes and provide justifications for their answers.
She further mentioned that in secondary schools, emphasis is placed on both calculator-assisted and non-calculator calculations.
This is intended to strike a balance between mental arithmetic skills – such as mental calculation and estimation – and the ability to solve more complex problems.
“As part of the RTPMM, we intend to develop an integrated virtual hub for teaching resources.
“This is designed to facilitate easier access to these materials for both teachers and students.
“This is because we actually possess a wealth of materials, and we aim to integrate these resources into a single platform that is easily accessible to both students and teachers,” she said.

Aszunarni stated that the mathematics education network will also be strengthened through the involvement of universities, agencies, the industry and community, who will share their expertise and demonstrate the application of mathematics across various fields.
She noted that efforts to foster students’ interest and confidence also require the support of school administrators, counsellors, teachers of other subjects and parents.
This includes incorporating mathematical elements into co-curricular activities and daily life — such as managing pocket money or measuring ingredients for cooking.
“In reality, one way to spark their interest in mathematics is to help them understand that mathematics is all around them.
“That is the most important thing.
“We want them to grasp that mathematics is everywhere.
“Only then will they be able to appreciate it, rather than feel afraid of it,” she said.

She added that the RTPMM will be implemented in phases: beginning with the strengthening of foundations and readiness; followed by enhancement and expansion; and finally moving towards consolidation and impact assessment — all with the goal of producing a mathematically literate generation. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: RTPMM stands for Rancangan Transformasi Pendidikan Matematik Malaysia, or the Malaysia Mathematics Education Transformation Plan.
IPG stands for Institut Pendidikan Guru, or the Teacher Education Institutes.
KP2027 stands for Kurikulum Persekolahan 2027, or the 2027 School Curriculum.

a0ab7b8598e01615: JAKARTA, Oct 22 — Indonesian police have named 11 companies as suspects in investigations into forest and land fires, including three foreign-invested firms, as authorities intensify enforcement against businesses linked to the blazes.

National Police Chief General Suyudi Ario Seto disclosed the figures on Wednesday, Antara reported, saying investigators had encountered no major obstacles but were not yet ready to identify the companies.
Suyudi said those held accountable could include not only the companies but also their owners and shareholders.

The investigations follow an earlier announcement by the police Criminal Investigation Agency that 98 reports involving corporations linked to forest fires had been upgraded to the formal investigation stage.
Police are expected to disclose further suspects as evidence is gathered and legal requirements are fulfilled.
Separately, the Forestry Ministry has suspended the permits of six more companies operating in Central Kalimantan, bringing the number of forestry firms facing administrative sanctions to 32.
Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said the six companies were also ordered to restore areas affected by fires.
The companies are PT Produk Kalimantan Jaya, PT Taiyong Engreen, PT Hutan Produk Lestari, PT Ramang Agro Lestari, PT Puspa Warna Cemerlang and PT Sinergi Hutan Sejati.
Their concessions cover a combined 201,391 hectares, including 7,531 hectares affected by recent fires.
The ministry’s sanctions now cover 32 companies managing more than 1.9 million hectares of concessions, of which 18,489 hectares have been affected by fires.
Raja Juli warned that the companies could also face criminal proceedings if investigations found evidence of deliberate wrongdoing or criminal intent.
279801e0ba9a8231: WASHINGTON, Oct 22 — Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites yesterday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet.
PHP sits underneath popular web design platforms, so the weaknesses potentially affect a vast range of websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services.

Wiz, one of the security firms that found the flaws, estimated that PHP runs about 70 percent of the world’s websites and said they rank “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history.”
The US National Security Agency told organizations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline.
Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed.
Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online.
The flaws “often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the NSA said in a statement on X.
Attackers could use them to take over web servers without needing a password.

Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the PHP Foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.

The discovery came amid a surge in software security disclosures driven by increasingly powerful AI models, with the number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 on track to roughly double last year’s record total.
PHP programmers released a fix yesterday.
“If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now,” the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.
Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI said on X that it considered the flaws “one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory,” adding that the discovery “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.”
Often and fast

Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who studies AI, said companies he talks to are struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to guard against AI-driven cyberattacks.
“Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast,” he wrote on X.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Details leaked online Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them.
In France, local government websites, including one for the Paris police, were made inaccessible at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said.

In the Netherlands, the national digital identity service DigiD, the website of the House of Representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity center went offline as a precaution, according to Dutch public broadcaster NOS.
In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate said its own cyber.gov.au site was among government websites affected by the flaws, according to Australian public broadcaster ABC.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, warned users they could see outages on its sites while it addressed the flaws, and said it had deliberately taken many of its supporting services offline until they could be safely patched.

Several Pokemon apps, including Pokemon HOME, Pokemon Champions and Pokemon Sleep, also went offline Wednesday for emergency maintenance, with Pokemon Sleep citing security measures, according to gaming news site Kotaku.
The operator of the hit Japanese game Umamusume said it was carrying out maintenance to fix a PHP vulnerability found in its servers. — AFP
a0f47a8eee19b521: THE legend of Puteri Gunung Ledang has been part of Mila Mohsin's life for as long as she can remember.
Long before stepping into the shoes of Gusti Puteri Retno Dumilah for 'Puteri Gunung Ledang The Musical', the story had already taken root in her childhood.
It was brought to life through the gentle bedtime lullabies her mother sang, sparking her young imagination.
"Thinking about it now, I'm realising my first ever memories of Puteri Gunung Ledang were in my childhood bedroom," Mila recalls.
"Every night, my brother and I would look forward to hearing our mother sing us to sleep with her 'tembangs'."
Those Javanese songs offered far more than just comfort. Even at age 7, Mila vividly imagined the grandeur and weight of Majapahit history.
Slowly, she began to understand the significance of the world her mother, Puan Seri Tiara Jacquelina, had poured her heart into as an artiste.
Now, with Tiara directing the 2026 staging of the musical, Mila is discovering the legend from a completely new angle.
She is no longer the young daughter watching from the sidelines, but the lead performer responsible for breathing new life into one of Malaysia's most famous theatrical characters.
A STELLAR CAST
Running from Oct 31 to Nov 15 at the Jeffrey Cheah Performing Arts Centre in Sunway Square, the production features a star-studded ensemble.

Singer-songwriter Aisha Retno shares the role of Puteri Gunung Ledang, while Aqasha stars as Hang Tuah. Luqman Hafidz portrays the Sultan of Melaka, Yusof Hashim plays Gusti Adipati, and Mimi Fly and Nadia Aqilah share the role of Bayan.
For 30-year-old Mila, whose full name is Hani Karmila Hani Mohsin, the main challenge was not to copy her mother's famous performance, but to understand the Puteri on her own terms.

Although Tiara played the iconic princess, Mila has always viewed their interpretations as two distinct entities. Even so, growing up around the show gave her a deep, personal connection to the character's spirit.
"To me, she has always represented the most divine feminine energy: one of silent strength, measured power and unrelenting love," she says.
If she had to describe her own Puteri in three simple words, it would be curious, passionate and fearless.
OVERCOMING DOUBTS

But preparing for the role has been far from easy. Musical theatre requires actors to sing, dance and tell a moving story all at once — all while carrying the emotional and historical weight of the legend.
For someone who admits to being highly self-critical, the process can feel overwhelming. Her deep familiarity with earlier versions of the show created another hurdle.
Mila had to resist copying established choices, focusing instead on playing the character with a fresh mind.
"That meant finding ways to dismiss the colossal expectations others have put on me and deciding the only thing that matters is doing right by Gusti Puteri," she explains.

She has also had to master the power of quiet moments on stage — learning to let a scene breathe rather than forcing an emotion or movement. It's a lesson that mirrors the princess herself, whose true power lies in quiet clarity rather than loud defiance.
For Mila, the heart of the story is freedom: the freedom to choose, to love and to stay true to oneself.
She draws strong inspiration from Srikandi, the brave warrior princess revered in Javanese tradition.
"I take much inspiration from Srikandi," she says.
"Like Srikandi, my version of Puteri will always fight from a place of justice and compassion. Not just 'love', but compassion."
That distinction is vital to her. Her Puteri is not just a tragic romantic figure, but a warrior guided by deep principle.
"Puteri's refusal to be another victim of the status quo is what makes her an icon until today," she says, adding that the character shaped her early understanding of feminism.

"Her willpower, self-worth and sense of justice are something I keep with me wherever I go. I feel those aspects will transcend time and always resonate. After all, a big part of being human is fighting for what you believe is right."
PERSPECTIVE AND COLLABORATION
Playing the princess has also helped Mila put her own life into perspective. She is now far more mindful of not letting minor setbacks or opinions overwhelm her.
Sometimes, she reminds herself, the Puteri was simply a young woman curious about the world outside her palace, who had to live with the choices she made.
"It's for this reason that I believe every moment is a choice, and we should take an active part in making them, rather than simply accept what is suggested to us," she reflects.
Sharing the leading role with Aisha Retno has further enriched the experience. Though similar in age, Mila feels their different backgrounds bring unique layers to the character.
Watching another actor approach the same scenes offers fresh insights she might have otherwise missed.
"Together, I feel we're able to present the most complete picture of Gusti Puteri for audiences to understand," she says.
MOTHER'S TUTELEGE

The production marks the first time the mother and daughter are working together as director and performer. Despite the potential complications of mixing family life with work, Mila says the experience has been wonderfully rewarding.
"I've always known her to be the strongest and most determined woman, but as an artiste it is tenfold. She insists. She is relentless. She prevails," she says of Tiara.
Having tasted the immense demands of the role herself, Mila now holds an even deeper respect for what her mother achieved over the years.

Watching Tiara direct has revealed a whole new level of that dedication. Their working relationship relies on one shared goal: doing what is best for the production. That clarity has built total trust between them.
Mila quickly clears up any doubts about favouritism. Being the director's daughter brings zero perks in the rehearsal room.
"I also get criticised and given notes, just like all the other cast members in PGL, even though I'm the type who likes to do my homework," she says.
Tiara's feedback to Mila and co-star Aqasha often focuses on staying fully present in the moment — building a genuine, living connection on stage rather than acting out a rigid routine.
Outside the theatre, the pair keep work and personal life strictly separate. Dinner conversations, for example, are kept completely free of rehearsal talk.
"As a director, she trusts me, and I trust her. Everything runs smoothly," Mila says.
Despite comparisons, Mila feels no bitterness. She accepts that audiences naturally compare a new actor to an iconic past performance.
She focuses on meeting her own high standards while honouring the show's rich legacy.
"My mother and I are very different people and, therefore, different performers," she points out.
"At the end of the day, I know in my heart the best way to honour my mother's legacy is not to try to live up to her achievements, but rather to carve my own path alongside her."

As opening night approaches, Mila's journey is about much more than taking over a famous role. It is about rediscovering a cherished story through her own eyes, stepping into her own strength and showing that a great legacy doesn't need to be cloned — only genuinely felt.
For Mila, the ultimate tribute to the Puteri — and to her mother — is having the courage to stand proudly in her own shoes.

4bbdadb0b809719a: MALÉ: Standing among the offices, shops and tightly packed streets of the Maldivian capital Malé is Hukuru Miskiiy, or the Old Friday Mosque - a nearly 400-year-old place of worship built largely from blocks of coral stone, its walls covered with delicate carvings and Arabic calligraphy.

For travellers accustomed to images of turquoise lagoons, white beaches and luxury resorts, the mosque reveals another side of the Maldives. Here, the country's Islamic history is not confined to museums or monuments; it remains woven into the daily rhythm of the city.

When the call to prayer sounds, civil servants, shopkeepers and other residents begin arriving for congregational prayers. Imam Muhammad Haneef, 55, said the mosque can accommodate more than 100 worshippers at a time.

The present Hukuru Miskiiy was completed in 1657 under Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar I, although earlier mosques had occupied the site for centuries. The first was built in the 12th century after the Maldives embraced Islam in 1153, while another followed in 1338.

By the 17th century, the growing congregation required a larger structure. With conventional building stone scarce on the islands, Maldivian craftsmen turned to something available in abundance: coral.

Blocks of Porites coral were cut and fitted together by hand, using an interlocking method that allowed the rough, porous surfaces to grip one another tightly. Nearly four centuries later, much of that craftsmanship remains clearly visible.

The mosque walls are covered with geometric patterns, floral designs, Arabic calligraphy and examples of Dhives Akuru, an old Maldivian script. Some carvings have softened with age, but enough remains to appreciate the extraordinary patience involved in creating them without modern machinery.

The use of coral gives the building a character quite unlike the grand marble mosques found elsewhere in the Islamic world. Its beauty is quieter and more tactile: weathered stone, deeply carved surfaces and centuries of salt air.

Inside, the material changes but the attention to detail does not. Timber dominates the upper portions of the mosque, from its multi-tiered roof to its doors, windows and frames, with sandalwood among the materials used and intricate carving and lacquer work displaying another side of traditional Maldivian craftsmanship.

Some of the mosque's sliding doors and windows still operate without wheels despite being almost 400 years old. Quranic verses and Arabic calligraphy appear throughout the interior, linking decoration with the building's religious purpose.

An unexpected detail also awaits worshippers: the mosque itself is not aligned directly with the qibla, the direction Muslims face during prayer. Instead, worshippers stand at an angle of about 30 degrees to the building, following a line inside the prayer hall that points towards Makkah.

One theory is that the site had previously been occupied by a Buddhist temple, reflecting the Maldives' pre-Islamic history. Buddhism was practised in the islands before their conversion to Islam in the 12th century.

Beside Hukuru Miskiiy stands another reminder of how dramatically Malé has changed. The mosque's coral-stone tower, known as the Munnaaru, was built in 1675 and rises about 11m; before modern high-rises crowded the capital, it was one of the most prominent landmarks on the island.

It is said that Malé could once be viewed almost from end to end from the top. Today, the tower sits amidst a far denser cityscape, surrounded by multistorey buildings that would have been unimaginable to those who built it.
The mosque grounds also contain four centuries-old wells and a cemetery where former rulers and members of the Maldivian royal family are buried, including Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar I.

Together, these details make Hukuru Miskiiy feel less like an isolated historic attraction and more like a condensed history of Malé itself. The Maldives marked 900 years since its conversion to Islam this year, with heritage preservation among the themes of the anniversary.

That long history is perhaps easiest to understand somewhere like Hukuru Miskiiy, where centuries-old coral carvings share space with worshippers arriving for afternoon prayers. In one of the world's most densely built capitals, the survival of a hand-carved coral house of worship from 1657 feels remarkable in and of itself.
002e5577aa298cd4: Untuk seketika, perkataan ‘paling bodoh’ menjadi kata kunci yang masyhur. Ini ekoran seorang siswi Fakulti Ekonomi daripada Universiti Malaya (UM) bernama Ummi Umairah Bakhit menyelar tindakan segelintir Melayu yang menderma wang hasil titik peluh untuk membantu golongan elit disabitkan kes rasuah. Ummi menyatakan perbuatan tersebut adalah sesuatu yang paling bodoh selain tidak bermoral. Kenyataan, atau lebih tepat soalan Ummi tersebut dilontarkan ketika acara dalam sebuah forum terbuka yang menampilkan panel antara lain seorang DJ terkenal, Menteri Besar Johor Onn Hafiz Ghazi dan Menteri Besar Selangor Amirudin Shari. Forum itu adalah sebahagian daripada acara Sidang Kemuncak Pemimpin Muda Masa Depan Antarabangsa di Kuala Lumpur.

Dalam pertanyaan Ummi itu, beliau mempersoalkan tindakan sesetengah orang yang memilih menderma bagi membantu pesalah rasuah, Najib Razak, untuk membayar denda mahkamah berjumlah RM50 juta bagi membolehkan dirinya layak menjadi tahanan di rumah. Suis ketokohan Onn Hafiz nampak off atau terpadam seketika manakala DJ terkenal dalam forum tersebut nampaknya tersangkak, gugup lagi gagap untuk menjawab soalan yang tidak dijangka itu.

Bukan sahaja kata bodoh, sebetulnya Ummi mempertikaikan tindakan mempertahankan rasuah dan korupsi dengan menyebut-nyebut perihal skandal Tabung Haji dan lain-lain. Ini adalah intipati yang sepatutnya menjadi sorotan.

Meskipun berbahasa Inggeris, kata bodoh yang digunakan memang menular menjadi racun dalam pembuluh darah ramai penyokong Najib. Selepas keratan video itu menjadi tular, ramai dalam kalangan ahli Umno di media sosial ‘menghunus keris’ kepada siswi ini. Ada yang malah meminta Universiti Malaya mengambil tindakan terhadap beliau. Ummi malah diugut, diancam dan dinista. Padahal kata-kata Ummi menistai perbuatan rasuah itu adalah sesuatu yang terpuji.

Setelah ancaman terhadap Ummi menjadi-jadi, Menteri Pendidikan Tinggi Zambry Abdul Kadir akhirnya menegaskan mahasiswa mempunyai hak untuk bersuara dan tiada sebarang tindakan tatatertib akan dikenakan terhadapnya susulan pertanyaan kritis mengenai dana sumbangan Najib itu. Noor Azuan Abu Osman, naib canselor Universiti Malaya turut terpaksa tampil memberikan kenyataan rasmi yang senada.

Kenyataan kedua-dua tokoh besar dalam pengajian tinggi ini amat penting. Ini kerana bekas naib canselor Universiti Malaya antara tahun 1988 sehingga 1991, Syed Hussein Alatas iaitu seorang pemikir, yang karya masyhurnya bertajuk ‘Rasuah: Sifat, Sebab dan Fungsi’ pernah mempopularkan satu terma berkesan. Terma tersebut ialah gejala bebalisme. Ia datang daripada kata bebal, yang secara mudahnya bermaksud bodoh. Malah bebal adalah lebih dahsyat daripada bodoh. Ia adalah satu kalimat yang menunjukkan tumpul otak, sukar mengerti, lambat menanggapi atau memahami sesuatu perkara, dan menurut Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka membawa juga pengertian melakukan aneka kesalahan berulang.

Akan tetapi apakah yang dimaksudkan oleh Syed Hussein yang terkenal benci rasuah dan perasuah itu dengan kata ‘bebal’. Beliau mula memperkenalkan istilah bebalisme dalam Dewan Masyarakat edisi Mac 1988.

Menurut Syed Hussei, bebalisme ini ‘bukan satu ideologi atau sistem kepercayaan atau kebudayaan atau falsafah’ tetapi ia adalah ‘orientasi pemikiran yang malas, tidak berfikir, tidak berlogik, kadang-kadang kasar, tidak ambil tahu, terlalu cepat percaya tanpa bukti, tidak saintifik, berhamburan, tiada haluan, pasif, tidak kreatif dan tiada tujuan yang terang.’

Semua anasir yang beliau sebutkan di atas akan kita jumpa di media sosial. Kita akan temukan di Facebook, X, Tiktok dan Threads. Apa sahaja yang disalurkan akan diulas sebagai satu komentar, atau ditelan bulat dan lonjong tanpa sebarang daya kritis. Tuduhan, fitnah, dakwaan palsu membiak dan beranak pinak dengan mudah di musim politik bergelora. Gejala bebalisme ini akan mudah dieksploitasi oleh pihak bertentangan dalam politik. Masing-masing akan menyebar informasi yang entah ya entah tidak.

Syed Hussein seterusnya mengatakan ‘bebalisme adalah lintah bagi pemikiran’. Ia tidak perlu diajarkan, atau dikemukakan secara teratur. Ia terjadi dengan sendiri dan ‘disebarkan sebagai satu trend’ dan ia dirujuk sebagai lintah oleh beliau lantaran pelaku atau si bebalis itu ‘bertindak melalui mental tanpa kesedaran’.

Oleh sebab ia adalah lintah bagi pemikiran, ia boleh melekap pada siapa pun. Kata Syed Hussein, ia ‘berada dalam berbagai-bagai golongan masyarakat; tidak kira umur, jantina, kebudayaan, bangsa, agama, falsafah, keadaan, waktu dan tempat’.

Apa yang menggerunkan ia adalah unsur utama yang menghalang pertumbuhan intelektual. Makanya, apabila penyokong Umno ramai-ramai ingin membantai Ummi, kita segera tahu dan mengesani bahawa rata-rata orang Umno ini terkait dengan fenomena bebalisme yang membimbangkan ini. Mungkin tidak semua, misalnya Zambry yang juga ahli Umno.
Syed Hussein juga mengaitkan bebalisme dengan ‘aliran fanatik’ iaitu mereka yang enggan menerima kebenaran dan fakta, dan terus-terusan memilih untuk percaya hal-hal bodoh dan tanpa dasar.
Apakah ciri-ciri bebalisme dan mereka yang menghidapinya, iaitu bebalis?

Menurut Syed Hussein, sang bebalis itu adalah; pertamanya mempertahankan kejahilan dan kedegilan. Keduanya mereka itu pemalas, enggan mengikuti hujah dan menganalisanya. Ketiganya, mereka selalunya bersikap acuh tak acuh, berbanding dengan daya usaha yang gigih dalam berfikir. Yang mana apa sahaja lambakan penipuan dan perdaya akan ‘diterima, berbagai-bagai pendapat, berbagai-bagai khurafat, berbagai- bagai keanehan dan keganjilan’.

Keempat, bebalisme ini menjelma kerana ada rasa diri itu ‘bersifat berkuasa benar (authoritarian) yang mana ini benar pada sesetengah ahli politik yang berasa mereka masih berkuasa atau lebih berkuasa dari rakyat. Itulah sebabnya dalam hal Ummi kita melihat beliau dibuli di dalam talian.
Kelima, mereka yang bebal itu ‘tidak suka merenung dan berfikir dan tidak suka menguji (non-experimental)’.

Keenamnya, tambah Syed Hussein, ‘satu ciri bebalisme adalah menghendaki orang lain mempercayai apa yang disarankan atau diperkatakan tanpa memberi sebab-sebab atau penjelasan yang cukup mengenai sesuatu yang luar daripada kebiasaan’.

Ketujuh, Syed Hussein sosiologis terkemuka negara pernah menulis, ‘bebalisme tidak suka kepada sifat teratur dan perbahasan secara rasional dan tidak menghargai kedua-duanya sama sekali. Apabila seorang bebalis bertindak secara rasional, ini adalah kerana pengaruh daripada kebiasaan dan bukan pemikiran mendalam secara rasional dan kerana terapan agama atau kuasa luar.’ Jika kita merenung ciri ini, kita akan mendapati terdapat sesetengah penyokong agamawan atau tokoh kanan tertentu gagal berfikir waras kerana hati serta penglihatan mereka telah dibutakan oleh ketaasuban.

Kelapan, golongan bebal ini akan cepat kita kesani iaitu ’apabila mereka bertanya, ia menampakkan kurangnya kefahaman mereka tentang prinsip-prinsip dan dengan itu soalan mereka menjadi sia-sia.’ Sebagai contoh dalam hal isu kepimpinan adat dan pertikaian kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, apa sahaja fakta yang dibawa bahawa Undang yang lama telah digantikan di Luak dan disahkan di Dewan Keadilan akan kekal dinafikan, dipermainkan dan ditolak. Mereka enggan berusaha mempelajari prinsip adat sedia ada, dan terus-terusan menghasut, memprovokasi dan mencabar institusi adat dan diraja di negeri itu.

Dan kesembilan, Syed Hussein mengatakan sang bebalis itu biasanya ‘antilogik, kusut pemikiran, subur dengan kurafat, tidak mengandungi rasa seni (unaesthetic), tidak mempunyai sikap memelihara, menerima segala sesuatu tanpa menimbang dengan akal, tidak mempedulikan hukum sebab (causation) dan hukum pertentangan (contradiction), bersikap kuasa-benar (authoritative), dan pemikiran malas, degil, serta buntu.’

Jika kita khuatir gejala bebalisme ini mewabak di Malaysia, kita perlu mengetahui mana asal puncanya. Apakah yang menyebabkan bebalisme ini? Menurut Syed Hussein ia bermula di rumah. Tulis beliau dalam rencana itu, ‘penghalang yang pertama ialah suasana di rumah'. Dalam erti kata lain, jika ibu bapa bodoh dan bengap, biasanya mereka gagal menumbuhkan suasana tidak bebal dalam rumah tangga. Alatas malahan mengatakan untuk mengetahui rumah itu penuh kebebalan atau tidak, memadai dinilai jika ‘keluarga terlalu menggalakkan sukan dan muzik’ dan ‘tidak membaca buku’. Ini kerana ‘pengetahuan intelektual tidak disanjung tinggi sebagaimana pengetahuan tentang agama dan adat’. Syed Hussein seterusnya menyatakan bukanlah setiap rumah perlu melahirkan intelektual; ‘walaupun kita tidak mengharap tiap-tiap orang atau tiap-tiap keluarga melahirkan watak intelektual, tetapi kita perlu berharap sebahagian keluarga dan anggota masyarakat dapat menghasilkan semangat intelektual tadi’.
Apa yang lebih menakutkan dalam masyarakat adalah bebalisme ini turut dibiakkan oleh ahli akademik yang mana itu perlu dibincangkan dalam tulisan lain.

Misalnya, Ketua Menteri Melaka, Ab Rauf Yusoh bakal menerima ijazah kedoktoran daripada Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) pada 21 Nov ini. Ketua menteri Melaka yang bakal bergelar doktor itu pernah menyeru penyokong dan rakyat yang menyayangi Najib supaya mengumpulkan dana bagi membantu melengkapkan RM 50 juta agar beliau dapat ditahan di rumah.

Mujur sangat-sangat bekas ketua hakim negara, Tengku Maimun Tuan Mat dilantik sebagai penyandang pertama Kursi Diraja Integriti dan Tadbir Urus Baik, UKM. Pelantikan beliau itu diperkenan dan dititahkan oleh Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz yang juga tersohor antirasuah dan korupsi.

Apa pun syukur nikmat Allah, ada Ummi Umairah Bakhit yang telah dididik dan diasuh di rumah yang betul, di sekolah yang betul, di universiti yang betul; dan membaca bahan-bahan yang betul sehingga mampu berfikir kritis dan tidak bodoh. Sebagai alumni Universiti Malaya saya berbangga dengan Ummi. Tambahan pengungkap kata Syed Hussein adalah sarjana di Universiti Malaya dan pernah menjadi felo penyelidik kanan di Institut Alam dan Tamadun Melayu (Atma) di UKM suatu masa dahulu.
Pun berapa ramai generasi baharu seperti Ummi Umairah Bakhit? Berapa ramai yang mengenali Syed Hussein Alatas. Buka media sosial anda dan lihat berapa dan betapa ramai bebalis di luar sana.

dc2ecfeed8750825: From Moaz Nair

The persistent, fractured politicking among Indian political leaders has devolved into a tragic spectacle of self-preservation, birthing a swarm of toothless, ego-driven factions that have completely abandoned the community’s most vulnerable.
For decades, these leaders have traded genuine community advancement for personal clout and minor cabinet crumbs, leaving working-class Indians politically homeless.

Ironically, as the Indian demographic footprint shrinks, the number of these redundant, self-serving political groups keeps multiplying — each shouting from its own small hill while achieving absolutely nothing of substance.

If these career politicians truly possess an ounce of genuine care for the marginalised, they must immediately halt their petty bickering, dismantle their hollow factions, and focus on delivering institutional, non-negotiable economic welfare.

Recent demographic data from the statistics department covering 2016 to 2026 lays bare a damning reality. In just one decade, the Indian component of the citizen population shrivelled from 7% to 6.5%. Representing roughly 5.8% of the total national population, ethnic Indians total about 2.1 million citizens.
Behind these dwindling percentages lies an unsettling truth: a minority community is fast becoming adrift from the mainstream of national development.

Approximately 38.7% of the community falls into the Bottom 40% (B40) income bracket, translating to 227,000 households. More alarming still, the data indicates that 10% of these B40 families — around 22,000 households — survive on less than RM2,000 a month in extreme precarity.
However, a shrinking population footprint must never be used as a political excuse for a diminished national commitment.

Instead, this demographic decline demands an immediate paradigm shift — shattering the status quo of lazy, generic handouts and replacing them with high-impact policy interventions built upon three non-negotiable pillars.
The 2027 budget attempts to tackle these imbalances, but its success will hinge on execution.
Equity, asset ownership, and economic empowerment

A shrinking population share inherently dilutes purchasing power and locks minority communities out of wealth accumulation. To bridge this widening wealth chasm, outdated asset ownership policies must be aggressively dismantled.
This means enforcing strict, mandatory quotas and dedicated housing funds to guarantee B40 Indian households affordable housing.
The 2027 budget confronts these capital deficits by channelling a combined RM150 million through Tekun Nasional and Amanah Ikhtiar Malaysia.

This includes a dedicated RM100 million Indian Community Entrepreneur Development Scheme to provide critical capital to small business owners, and RM50 million in microcredit loans customised to uplift Indian women entrepreneurs.
Ensuring families own homes and hold financial assets is vital to systematically engineering sustainable, multi-generational social mobility.
TVET overhaul and educational infrastructure

A radical technical and vocational education and training (TVET) overhaul and digital empowerment must disrupt a stagnant workforce. The brutal job market of tomorrow will show no mercy to obsolete skillsets.
Indian youth — particularly those trapped in forgotten suburban fringes and estates — must be aggressively channelled into high-tier TVET ecosystems.

The 2027 budget offers a vital fiscal upgrade here. The allocation for the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) has been boosted to RM150 million, specifically earmarked to help youths make the transition into high-skilled industrial pipelines. Furthermore, Indian youth must tap into the wider national RM8 billion TVET budget.

Equally foundational is confronting the historical deficits in education infrastructure. Malaysia’s 528 Tamil national-type primary schools (SJKT) carry a complex legacy, with 324 operating as government-assisted institutions sitting on private estate or community trust lands.

This has historically locked many schools out of direct development funding, leaving 68% of them without basic ICT laboratories. The 2027 budget addresses this digital divide with a RM50 million allocation for essential repairs, rewiring, and basic amenities, alongside full reconstruction priorities for severe emergencies like SJKT Dengkil in Selangor and SJKT Gopeng in Perak.
Ruthless structural reform for targeted poverty alleviation
The survival of these policies hinges entirely on a ruthless structural reform of Mitra. For decades, fragmented agendas and redundant aid distribution have sabotaged state interventions.

Mitra must be stripped of bureaucracy and given absolute, transparent, and centralised power over data, funding, and execution. Armed with a unified database, cost-of-living aid, scholarships, and micro-business grants can finally bypass bureaucratic gridlock.

Crucially, the ultimate success of the budget for working-class Indians relies on broader macroeconomic shifts. The mandated minimum wage hike to RM2,000 per month starting June 2027 will immediately lift the community’s most vulnerable 22,000 households out of deep financial distress, especially when combined with the RM16 billion Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah cash aid pool.
Moving beyond salvation

Ultimately, the integrity of Malaysia’s future will be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable. Addressing this demographic collapse is not a bloodless numbers game on a spreadsheet; it is an urgent battle for socioeconomic justice.
By executing these progressive policy pillars, the country can transform a demographic challenge into a powerful reservoir of human capital.

However, relying solely on external political salvation is a failing strategy. If the Indian community is to survive as a relevant economic force in Malaysia’s shifting landscape, it must aggressively dismantle internal fatalism.

Upward mobility cannot be granted by policy alone. Real transformation demands that the community fiercely engineer its own self-upliftment — taking absolute ownership of its wealth, its trajectory, and its future generations.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

0d2b0cb5e7f78f1d: SYDNEY: A class action lawsuit has been filed in an Australian court against Meta Platforms' Facebook and Instagram, alleging that the social media platforms exposed children to harmful content and kept them hooked through algorithms.

The lawsuit, filed in the Federal Court of Australia, the country's second-highest court, by law firm MinterEllison this month, could be the first in Australia to hold social media responsible for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers.
The class action has been filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs, who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were under 18 and are seeking compensation.
Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information that could reveal the identities of the applicants or the contents of the statement of claim.
Meta agreed in August to pay US$18 billion to settle claims brought by nearly all US states that it had designed social media to addict children.

The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech following a world-first ban on social media for children under 16 and newly proposed rules that could allow users to switch off algorithm-driven content in their feeds.
751ffee3da39b906: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Thirty per cent of couples who intended to divorce reconciled after undergoing family counselling sessions managed by the National Population and Family Development Board (LPPKN).

Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development (KPWKM) secretary-general Datuk Dr Maziah Che Yusoff said the achievement demonstrated that counselling could help couples better understand domestic conflicts and reconsider their decision to separate.

“Although the rate may seem small, it is a significant achievement for us, considering that the initiative only began last year,” she said while appearing as a guest on the Kasih Lensa Keluarga podcast produced by Bernama TV at Wisma Bernama yesterday.
She said poor communication between husbands and wives was among the main causes of domestic conflict.
Counselling sessions provide a space for couples to manage their emotions, communicate openly and reassess the impact of their conflicts on their marriage and their children’s future.

“Sometimes, the root cause of a dispute is not particularly significant, yet it affects the emotions of both parties. When a couple sits down to discuss matters calmly, they can see the bigger picture regarding the future of their family and marriage,” she said.
Maziah said KPWKM would continue to improve family intervention services based on findings and experiences from existing programmes.
She said efforts to strengthen the family institution were central to the National Family Compassion Policy (DKKN) 2026-2030, launched by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim on Feb 14.
The policy translates the National Social Policy into efforts to address increasingly complex family challenges and social issues.

“DKKN is based on five core Kasih values, namely Affection (Kasih Sayang), Trust (Amanah), Health (Sihat), Knowledge (Ilmu) and Harmony (Harmoni). It also encompasses five strategic thrusts involving the marriage institution, family planning, parenting quality, inclusive family support and conflict management,” she said.
Commenting on modern parenting challenges, Maziah said children were influenced not only by their home environment but also by digital technology, social media, schools and peers.
“In the past, a well-behaved child would simply stay at home. Today, however, a child alone in their room is not necessarily safe from outside influences because of smartphones,” she said.
She said strengthening the family institution required cooperation among the government, communities and schools, rather than placing the entire responsibility on parents.
Meanwhile, she invited the public to attend the National Family Day celebration in Shah Alam on Nov 6 and 7, which will feature various family-related programmes and exhibitions. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: LPPKN stands for Lembaga Penduduk dan Pembangunan Keluarga Negara, or the National Population and Family Development Board.
KPWKM stands for Kementerian Pembangunan Wanita, Keluarga dan Masyarakat, or the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development.
DKKN stands for Dasar Kasih Keluarga Negara, or the National Family Compassion Policy.

f1c0ae2a08fedeba: OCTOBER 22 — The Education Ministry recently released figures: 5,681 bullying cases reported in schools between January and August this year. The Prime Minister himself admitted the real number is “definitely higher.”
It’s disheartening. CCTV cameras have been installed. Police have been sent into schools. Counsellors have been added. So why does the bullying keep happening?
Let me say something uncomfortable but necessary: we’ve been treating a human problem with a surveillance mindset.

Cameras cover corridors and corners. They don’t cover the punch thrown in the toilet, or the note passed under the desk with something cruel written on it. Police can arrest a perpetrator, but they can’t arrest the fear a child carries walking into class every morning. The PM himself noted that the school in Yong Peng had cameras — but “not where it happened.” That line is a metaphor: the real bullying hotspots have never been within camera range.

This isn’t uniquely Malaysian. Unesco data across 144 countries shows 32 per cent of students were bullied in the month before being surveyed. South Korea bars students with bullying records from university entrance exams. Japan reported nearly 770,000 bullying incidents in fiscal 2024. Germany: nearly half of teenagers say they’ve been bullied. But here’s what stands out: 27 per cent of Malaysian students report being bullied, against an OECD average of 20 per cent. On being mocked by classmates, we’re at 44 per cent versus 35 per cent.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Bullying never happens in a vacuum. It happens where adult attention is absent. — artempodrez/Pexels pic
We’re not the worst. But we’re noticeably worse than average.
So where’s the problem? I think there’s a key issue being overlooked: schools have lost the ability — and the space — to solve their own problems.

Right now, the ministry issues a circular, schools execute it. The ministry adds a system, teachers fill in data. Teachers are drowning in non-teaching work. The National Union of the Teaching Profession (NUTP) says the main cause of teacher burnout is “not teaching itself” — it’s admin, reports, data entry, meetings, committees, co-curricular activities, and endless parent WhatsApp messages. iGuru has even proposed “One In One Out” — for every new task added, scrap an old one.

Think about it. A teacher juggling three or four systems, replying to dozens of parent messages, rushing reports — how much energy does he have left to notice the kid in class who’s suddenly gone quiet? How much patience to deal with friction between two students that “doesn’t count as serious”?
Bullying never happens in a vacuum. It happens where adult attention is absent.

I’m not saying the ministry shouldn’t be involved. Curriculum standards, teacher standards, safety floors — those must be set centrally. But “how to run things” and “what to teach” are two different questions. England’s school autonomy reforms offer a useful lesson: the state sets curriculum standards, but schools hire their own staff, set their own budgets, buy their own training. Local authorities provide “support on demand.” Schools get room to judge based on their own students’ needs.

Malaysia’s problem isn’t “too much direction.” It’s too much direction and too little trust. Every circular carries an implicit message: “You can’t do this, so I’ll tell you how.” Schools become execution terminals rather than educational communities with judgment.

G25’s statement hit the mark: the current approach is “reactive” — add measures after a crisis, wait for the next tragedy once the heat dies down. Cameras, security guards, disciplinary procedures are “necessary but don’t touch the root.”

What’s the root? Kids growing up in an increasingly challenging environment. Academic competition. Violence on social media. Dual-income parents with no time. Schools that offer little beyond grades in terms of belonging and meaning. None of that shows up on camera. No police officer can manage it. No circular can solve it.
The only people who can see it are the teachers who spend every day with these kids. If teachers are buried in admin, that last line of defence is gone.

So my view is simple: strip away what teachers don’t need to do. Give the space back to them. Let schools have the power to allocate resources and design interventions based on their own situation — instead of waiting for the next circular from the ministry. And tie “accountability” to “autonomy”: you give schools freedom, schools answer for student safety and growth. Data transparent. Results made public.

Giving schools autonomy isn’t dumping responsibility. It’s acknowledging a basic truth: the people closest to the children know best how to help them. This is the crux of the recommendation of a new book Breaking but Not Broken published by the MCKK Foundation. Malaysians are encouraged to read the book and offer further refinements. MCKK Foundation is hosting follow-up public discourses to further share. Those interested can join one on October 11 at the Publica Art Gallery.
