3d8e0bf794b0f520: PETALING JAYA: Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad’s khalwat (close proximity) controversy is unlikely to cost him support among Bersama’s followers, who tend to separate a politician’s private life from his political record, analysts say.
However, the controversy could make it harder for the PKR-splinter party to win over conservative Malays as it seeks to expand its voter base.

“No, it is not the end of his political career,” University of Tasmania academic James Chin told FMT, saying supporters of multiracial parties generally understand the need to separate a politician’s private life from politics.
Chin said several politicians had survived similar controversies previously, citing Amanah president Mohamad Sabu and former MCA president Dr Chua Soi Lek.

Mohamad Sabu, then a PAS Youth leader, was charged with khalwat in 1995 but was acquitted by the Kelantan shariah court without his defence being called after the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case. In 2011, he was elected the party’s deputy president.
Chua, on the other hand, resigned from all government and party posts in 2008 after being embroiled in a sex scandal, but staged a political comeback two years later, winning the MCA presidency.
Comebacks, following a controversy, are therefore possible, Chin said.
“A lot depends on which party you come from. You may not be able to come back if you're from PAS, but if you’re from DAP or PKR, it's really not a problem.”
Nik Nazmi, a co-leader of Bersama, confirmed on Saturday that he and a woman were detained by the Selangor Islamic religious department (Jais) in Petaling Jaya on Thursday for suspected khalwat.
Following the incident, the former Setiawangsa MP was suspended by his party for three months.

Likewise, Syaza Shukri of International Islamic University Malaysia agreed that the controversy was unlikely to cause lasting political damage, although such scandals could hurt politicians in the short term, particularly close to an election.
She said sex-related scandals generally trigger greater sensitivities among Malay voters than financial scandals, as they are closely linked to the leader’s “dignity and honour”.
Syaza said the bigger problem for Bersama was attracting new Malay voters rather than losing existing supporters, as the party does not have a large Malay support base to begin with.
“This incident would make it harder for them to win over undecided Malay voters,” she said, adding that retaining their existing support base was unlikely to be much of an issue.
Family plays role in political comeback
Both analysts said Nik Nazmi’s chances of making a comeback would also depend on his family’s response.
Chin says a comeback would be more likely if the former federal minister’s family does not abandon him.
“As long as the family remains silent, and no one talks about it, it will be forgiven,” Syaza said, adding that public support from Nik Nazmi’s wife could go a long way to helping him regain trust.
She said voters are entitled to scrutinise the private conduct of politicians, but should also allow them the opportunity to make amends.
“I think voters will be forgiving, especially if he takes the right steps.”

2881759ec3500584: LIMA: Forest fires fuelled by El Nino have killed 12 people and left hundreds homeless in Peru since June, authorities in the Andean country said Wednesday.
Most of the victims were farmers who died of injuries sustained trying to fight the flames, the National Emergency Operations Center, which goes by the Spanish acronym COEN, said.
The worst-affected region was Cusco, where a fire broke out close to the Inca citadel of Machu Picchu earlier this month.
A total of 457 forest fires were recorded in Peru between June and October.
Biologist Daniel Valle of the Scientific University of the South in Lima said that the flames spread quickly due to high temperatures and dry conditions caused by El Nino.
"We have a huge mass of hot, dry air over the whole of Peru as a result of El Nino," he told AFP.
The fires, which are often started by farmers who burn brush to clear land for crops, have consumed over 1,000 hectares of farmland and destroyed around a hundred homes.
A further 12,000 hectares of natural vegetation have also gone up in smoke.
On Wednesday, seven fires were burning in the Andes and the Peruvian Amazon, according to the COEN.

El Nino is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon that warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
This year's "Super" El Nino is set to peak in December, but is already wreaking havoc in some regions, including Central America, where animals are dying from drought.

6a042d7221d85a1f: WASHINGTON: The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Wednesday, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority," he added.

A diplomatic source in the Middle East told AFP that some families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, but Pigott stressed that Wednesday's order applied only to the departure of non-emergency embassy staff and their families in Saudi Arabia.

One person was killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, aviation officials said.

70cdef1e70b07704: WASHINGTON: The Philippines is exploring deeper cooperation with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables and addressing "gray-zone" activity, despite Manila's one-China policy, which recognises Beijing and not Taipei, a Philippine diplomat said on Wednesday.

"These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan," Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so "notwithstanding our one China policy".

Asked if this cooperation could include joint patrols or accountability for vessels that disrupt communications, Carino said he did not have details, but said: "I'm sure that this is a constantly evolving cooperation, and some of the things that you mentioned may be actually coming to fruition."

Taipei has stepped up efforts to protect undersea communications links, which are vital to the island's connections to the rest of the world, after several incidents involving cables and China-linked vessels.

This month, the Philippines' coast guard said it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge a Chinese research ship operating off northern Batanes province near undersea cable corridors.

ad9e4f2eec460218: SAINT PETERSBURG: Russia said Wednesday it was ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States after Vladimir Putin met a US envoy and freed a detained American - but Moscow played down the chances of a deal to end the conflict.
US president Donald Trump said it was "the closest we've been" to ending the war while his envoy Steve Witkoff praised Putin as a "humanitarian" for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard.
But the Kremlin warned after Witkoff's meeting with Putin in Saint Petersburg that there was little "substance" in the Ukrainian and European peace proposals that the US diplomat brought with him.
Witkoff had flown to Russia from a meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, which was aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between Zelensky and Trump.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the talks with Putin remotely.

Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, including AFP, that Russia was "in principle, ready to resume" the trilateral talks in mid-November - after crucial US midterm elections - and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on post-war security.
Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on "some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv" from the Oslo meeting, adding though that "there wasn't really much substance in them".
A summit between Putin, Trump and China's Xi Jinping was also being prepared in China's Shenzhen for next month, Ushakov said, calling it "the first such meeting in history."
'Work left to do'

During their three-hour meeting, Witkoff praised Putin for granting Trump's request to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian - you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," Witkoff said.

Witkoff said on social media afterward that the Putin talks were "constructive" but that "there is still important work left to do." Discussions would continue between the US, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added.
Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the Ukraine war in 24 hours - but over a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.

In recent days a frustrated Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Trump also delayed the imposition of sanctions on Russia's war machine - a decision he defended on Wednesday as necessary to secure Hubbard's release.
"If you would've put those sanctions on... you could forget about him. You'd never see him again," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Russian strikes kill four
Witkoff's ninth meeting with Putin came as Russia continued to pound Ukrainian cities ahead of winter.
Kyiv said Russian strikes killed at least four people - including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
Russian occupation authorities in the Lugansk region, meanwhile, said a Ukrainian drone strike on a phone company had killed two people.
In Ukraine, Zelensky said that Kyiv backed resuming trilateral talks.
"The American side is proposing to organise this meeting as soon as possible. We are in favour of it," he told journalists.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting Tuesday followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, and calls from Trump for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Witkoff told Putin he saw "some degree of momentum" in the US-led talks after meeting Zelensky in Oslo.
The US envoy also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for the diesel deal, which sparked outrage in Kyiv and across Europe.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterms, in which Trump's Republicans could lose control of Congress.

eaeb21251062467b: CAIRO: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was intended to "defend Saudi territory and does not include an attack on Yemen".
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said: "We are talking about defending the land and borders of the kingdom."
"The situation cannot bear any further instability in other countries. We want to restore the countries that have lost their stability," he added.
Sisi on Saturday asked parliament to authorise support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested".
The parliament, which is packed with supporters of the president, has since held two rare closed-door sessions before postponing deliberations until next week.
Following the morning event at which Sisi made the speech, which was reported later, a high-level Egyptian delegation visited Riyadh, the kingdom's state news agency reported.
Egypt's top diplomat Badr Abdelatty and spy chief Hassan Rashad delivered a letter from Sisi to Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi Press Agency said.
The contents of the message were not reported.
In recent weeks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing Riyadh to shut its main airport and postpone a major investment conference.
A Houthi maritime blockade is also threatening oil exports from the kingdom, the world's biggest crude exporter.

Saudi Arabia has since rallied support from its allies. French President Emmanuel Macron, on a surprise "solidarity" visit to the kingdom on Wednesday, said French troops would help shield the key oil terminal of Yanbu on the Red Sea.
The day before, the UK government announced it would deploy British fighter jets to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against increasing attacks.
Egypt's tightrope

A handful of dissenting voices in Egypt's parliament have demanded "specific objectives and clear information" on any possible deployment, as well as an assessment of the "potential risks to the lives of our soldiers".

Direct military involvement is unpopular in the Arab world's most populous nation, while memories remain of its last disastrous deployment in Yemen in the 1960s, when thousands of soldiers were killed fighting in the North Yemen civil war.
That mission, under President Gamal Abdel Nasser, was later compared with the US war in Vietnam.
Riyadh is one of Cairo's strongest allies and a key financial backer of Sisi's administration since the former army chief ousted Islamist president Mohammed Morsi in 2013.

In his speech on Saturday, Sisi said it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by as Riyadh's security and stability were threatened, given the unconditional support the kingdom had provided Egypt in the early days of his administration.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, contributing naval and air forces and deploying warships to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
But over the past decade, it has adopted an increasingly cautious foreign policy, prioritising its own national security.
It has positioned itself as a regional mediator, maintaining channels across conflict lines, including with Hamas, Israel and Iran.
On Wednesday, Abdelatty again said Egypt's foreign policy was defined by "wisdom and strategic balance".
This week, Abdelatty has been in contact with Iran's top diplomat, Abbas Araghchi, who has said that Egypt's potential involvement would make the situation "more difficult".
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," Araghchi said in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
Throughout this year, as its Gulf allies have come under attack in the war between Iran and the US, Cairo has repeatedly urged caution.
The Arab world's largest military did not issue a response even when its own Damietta port was struck by an unidentified drone in July.
It has not joined the Mecca defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in August, which experts said was intended to preserve its strategic autonomy.
Besides its close alliance with the kingdom, Egypt also has its own economic woes to consider.
Along with Saudi Arabia, Egypt has been hit hard by disruptions through Bab al-Mandab, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal, whose revenues have yet to recover since Houthi attacks began in 2023.

b30227d400d482cf: PETALING JAYA: Anyone who has endured the unpleasant experience of a filthy public toilet will appreciate the value of finding one that's clean, comfortable and properly maintained. Indeed, discovering an immaculate restroom while travelling can sometimes feel like striking gold.
Malaysia has been recognising establishments that take this humble amenity seriously, and the country's finest toilets have just received their moment in the spotlight.

The Toilet of the Year Awards 2026, held on Oct 20 in Kuala Lumpur, honoured eight winners across categories ranging from shopping centres and restaurants to petrol stations, schools and places of worship.
Organised by the housing and local government ministry, the competition attracted 849 entries, compared with 345 in its inaugural year in 2023.
Each category winner received RM20,000, a trophy and a certificate of recognition. So, which establishments have earned the distinction of offering some of Malaysia's finest facilities?
For shoppers, Sunway Square Mall in Subang, Selangor, took the honours, while Petronas Presint 18 in Putrajaya emerged victorious in the petrol-station category.
Travellers heading south along the North-South Expressway might want to remember the Seremban southbound rest and service area, which won the award for highway stops.

In Kuala Lumpur, The Lotas (MamaKim) in Desa Sri Hartamas secured the restaurant category, while Iconic Marjorie Penang, a Tribute Portfolio Hotel in Bayan Lepas, was recognised for its hotel facilities.
The winners weren't confined to commercial establishments: Masjid Nurussalam in Gerik, Perak took the award for places of worship, while SK Tok Randok in Ajil, Terengganu topped the school category.

Meanwhile, Shah Alam City Council earned recognition for the public toilet at Tasik Barat, Section 14, proving that municipal facilities can also hold their own against those in privately managed premises.
Together, the winners offer a geographical spread of establishments demonstrating that a decent restroom need not be an elusive luxury.
What makes a good toilet?
Although cleanliness is fundamental, a genuinely good public toilet also requires thoughtful design, reliable maintenance and facilities that accommodate different users.

Adequate lighting, functioning fixtures, accessible cubicles and sufficient supplies all contribute to an experience that visitors rarely celebrate when everything works - but certainly notice when something doesn't.
The awards form part of the ministry's broader Bersih, Menawan dan Wangi (BMW) initiative, which promotes toilets that are clean, attractive and pleasant-smelling.

Technology is also making its way into the country's restrooms: a recently introduced BMW-i smart toilet in Putrajaya, for example, features sensors that respond to odours, automated floor-drying systems and technology that records visitor numbers.
Such innovations may help improve maintenance, although sophisticated equipment alone is no substitute for consistent cleaning and responsible use.
A matter of national pride

The government has committed RM150 million between 2026 and 2030 to upgrading and maintaining public toilets managed by the local authorities. Housing and local government minister Nga Kor Ming also revealed that RM154 million had been channelled towards improving 1,529 public toilets between 2023 and 2025.

Speaking at the awards, he observed that public toilets were among the first facilities through which visitors formed impressions of a country. "They are our calling card and the frontline of a country's image," he said.
Next year's awards will introduce a ninth category for universities and other higher education institutions, expanding the recognition of establishments that maintain exemplary restrooms.
a2d9588558ac929a: Enam tahun lalu, menjelang PRN Sabah 2020, Perikatan Nasional (PN) memperkenalkan lambang yang kemudian menjadi identiti gabungan itu – tulisan putih 'PERIKATAN NASIONAL' dengan latar biru tua.

Logo itu diperkenalkan Muhyiddin Yassin pada 29 Ogos 2020 sebelum dilancarkan secara rasmi di Kota Kinabalu pada bulan berikutnya untuk digunakan dalam PRN Sabah. Ketika itu, PN masih sebuah jenama politik baru yang cuba menyatukan parti berbeza di bawah satu lambang.

Sejak itu, logo PN melalui beberapa pilihan raya dan semakin biasa dilihat pengundi. Antara ujian awalnya ialah PRN Melaka pada November 2021, apabila gabungan berkenaan bertanding di semua 28 kerusi DUN.

Hasilnya tidak memberangsangkan. PN sekadar menang dua kerusi, Sungai Udang menerusi Dr Mohd Aleef Yusof dan Bemban melalui Dr Mohd Yadzil Yaakub. Kedua-duanya ketika itu calon Bersatu manakala PAS kalah di semua lapan kerusi ditandinginya.
Namun, hanya setahun kemudian, kedudukan PN berubah dengan ketara.

Pada PRU15, gabungan itu memenangi 74 kerusi Parlimen. PAS menjadi penyumbang terbesar dengan 43 kerusi, manakala Bersatu mendapat 31. Bagi PAS, 43 kerusi itu pencapaian terbaik dalam sejarah penyertaannya dalam PRU.
Pencapaian itu menarik kerana ia tidak dibina dengan logo bulan semata-mata. Di Kelantan dan Terengganu, PN menggunakan lambang PAS, tetapi di banyak negeri lain calonnya bertanding di bawah logo PN.

Melaka antara contoh paling jelas. PAS yang sebelum itu tidak mempunyai kerusi Parlimen di negeri berkenaan berjaya menembusi Tangga Batu menerusi Bakri Jamaluddin dan Jasin menerusi Zulkifli Ismail. Kedua-duanya menang atas tiket PN, bukan menggunakan logo bulan.

Ia tidak bermakna logo menjadi satu-satunya sebab kemenangan. Kekuatan calon, jentera, isu semasa dan sentimen pengundi tetap memainkan peranan. Tetapi pengalaman PRU15 menunjukkan jenama PN sekurang-kurangnya dapat menjadi identiti bersama yang membawa PAS keluar daripada kawasan tradisinya.
Sebab itu pembatalan pendaftaran PN oleh Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia (JPPM) pada Selasa membawa masalah lebih besar daripada kehilangan satu lambang.

JPPM membatalkan pendaftaran gabungan itu selepas mendapati penjelasan dikemukakan PN gagal menyangkal asas pembatalan dalam notis terdahulu. PN sudah menyatakan akan mencabar keputusan itu melalui proses undang-undang dan turut mempertimbangkan rayuan kepada menteri dalam negeri.

Tetapi kalendar pilihan raya terus berjalan. Penamaan calon PRN Melaka ditetapkan pada 31 Okt, diikuti pengundian awal 10 Nov dan hari mengundi pada 14 Nov. Jika isu pendaftaran PN belum diselesaikan menjelang penamaan calon, komponennya perlu bersedia dengan pilihan lambang lain.
Bulan paling mudah dikenali
Antara pilihan yang sudah disebut secara terbuka ialah lambang PAS.
Ketua Pengarah Pilihan Raya PAS Sanusi Nor berkata tiada masalah untuk gabungan itu menggunakan logo PAS kerana lambang berkenaan sudah dikenali pengundi.

Dari segi pengenalan jenama, PAS mempunyai kelebihan yang sukar dinafikan. Bulan sudah digunakan parti itu selama beberapa dekad dan sangat sinonim dengan PAS, terutama di negeri seperti Kelantan, Terengganu dan Kedah.
Namun, masalahnya ialah Melaka bukan Kelantan atau Terengganu.

Penganalisis Mazlan Ali sebelum ini berkata, logo PAS paling dikenali antara pilihan yang ada jika PN tidak dapat menggunakan lambangnya, tetapi penggunaannya di luar kubu tradisi parti itu membawa cabaran, khususnya dalam menarik pengundi bukan Melayu dan di kerusi campuran.

Ahli akademik daripada Universiti Teknologi Malaysia itu juga berpandangan, parti lain dalam PN tidak menikmati tahap pengenalan lambang yang sama. Logo Gerakan kurang dikenali dalam kalangan pengundi Melayu, MIPP mempunyai tahap pengenalan lebih rendah, manakala Wawasan masih terlalu baru untuk pengundi benar-benar serasi dengannya.
Di sinilah dilema PAS muncul. Bulan ialah jenama kukuh, tetapi pencapaian terbaik parti itu di Melaka datang ketika dua calonnya membawa logo PN.
Wawasan ada tokoh tapi bagaimana dengan logo?
Pilihan lain ialah Wawasan.
Parti itu mempunyai barisan pemimpin berprofil tinggi. Hamzah Zainudin ialah presidennya, manakala bekas ketua menteri Melaka Rahim Thamby Chik antara naib presiden.

Tetapi usia jenama Wawasan masih singkat. Ia penjenamaan semula Parti Cinta Malaysia, dengan pertukaran nama dan logo mendapat kelulusan JPPM pada Julai lalu sebelum diterima secara rasmi sebagai komponen PN.
Tokoh terkenal boleh membantu membawa parti kepada perhatian umum, tetapi soal yang lebih besar ialah sejauh mana logo Wawasan sudah dikenali pengundi biasa menjelang hari mengundi.
Bagaimana pula ‘dacing’?
Ada satu lagi kemungkinan yang menjadikan persoalan logo ini lebih menarik – PAS bertanding menggunakan lambang Barisan Nasional (BN).

Presiden PAS Hadi Awang sebelum ini dilaporkan bersedia mempertimbangkan penggunaan logo BN pada PRN Melaka. Timbalannya Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man pula berkata PAS bersedia menggunakan lambang itu sekiranya langkah berkenaan dapat membantu memuktamadkan kerjasama dengan Umno.
Dari sudut Melaka sahaja, dacing mempunyai kelebihan sebagai lambang yang sudah lama dikenali pengundi. Tetapi implikasinya tidak semestinya berhenti selepas PRN.

Syaza Shukri daripada Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia sebelum ini membangkitkan soal timbal balik. Jika PAS sanggup menggunakan logo BN di Melaka, persoalan boleh timbul sama ada BN pula akan menuntut ruang serupa di negeri diterajui PAS pada masa depan.

Mazlan pula melihat kemungkinan timbul kerumitan jika hubungan kedua-dua parti berubah selepas calon PAS bertanding dengan logo dan watikah BN, manakala Azmi Hassan berkata aturan sedemikian juga boleh memberi BN modal tawar-menawar dalam rundingan kerusi menuju PRU16.

Justeru, keputusan mengenai lambang bukan sekadar soal mendapatkan logo untuk dicetak pada kertas undi 14 Nov. Ia turut menyentuh identiti, hubungan antara parti dan kedudukan dalam rundingan politik selepas Melaka.

Logo PN bermula di Sabah pada 2020 sebagai lambang kepada sebuah gabungan baharu. Enam tahun kemudian, ia sudah melalui kekalahan besar di Melaka dan kemuncak 74 kerusi pada PRU15 sehingga menjadi jenama politik yang dikenali.

Kini pembatalan pendaftarannya meletakkan satu persoalan yang sukar dielakkan: jika logo PN tidak dapat dibawa ke PRN Melaka, adakah pengundi yang selama ini memilih PN sanggup mengikutnya apabila ‘bulan’, Wawasan atau mungkin ‘dacing’ mengambil tempat di kertas undi?

e3f519129b2e62b1: Whenever a minimum wage announcement falls short of public expectations, the political knee-jerk reaction is to aim all arrows at Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Yet, directing the blame solely at him misses the real dynamics behind Malaysia’s wage policy formulation.

First, consider how policy recommendations are shaped. Talent Corp and the human resources ministry paid RM1 million to a consulting firm specifically to research and recommend an appropriate minimum wage rate.
When the government relies on external subject-matter experts, paid handsomely with public funds, it acts on structured economic assessments rather than arbitrary political whims.
If the resulting figure feels inadequate to the working public, we must scrutinise the methodology, data and assumptions used by these highly paid consultants first.
The research, findings, and identity of these consultants ought to be made public for full transparency and proper scrutiny before rushing to condemn the prime minister.

Second, the relentless pushback from employer groups continues to stall wage growth. Business associations and industry groups routinely lobby against wage increases, warning of economic ruin and mass layoffs.

Their aggressive pushback invariably leads to exemptions and now deferred compliance for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), diluting the impact of wage reforms across major sectors of the economy.
Meanwhile, Anwar’s track record demonstrates a consistent commitment to raising worker compensation.
The minimum wage has risen 33% under the Madani government from RM1,500 in 2022 to RM2,000 in 2027. Graduates and semi-skilled workers will have a new minimum monthly salary of RM2,500.

Under Anwar’s administration, government-linked companies (GLCs) have actively led by example, setting a baseline living wage that was raised in Budget 2027 from RM3,100 to RM3,400. This upward revision reflects a genuine drive to ensure decent standards of living where the government holds direct leverage.

The true obstacles to a higher floor wage are not found in the prime minister’s office. The real villains in this story are the corporate lobbies constantly fighting wage increases and the consultants who produce conservative recommendations despite million-ringgit fees.

Rather than make Anwar the scapegoat, public discourse should demand accountability from the consultants who drafted the proposal and the employer groups who consistently undermine fair pay for Malaysian workers.

That said, according to research and analysis published in The Economist, governments should be cautious about aggressive minimum wage hikes due to mounting evidence of hidden economic distortions and better alternative policy tools.

Research from Nobel Prize winner David Card and others in the 1990s showed that the negative impact of minimum wages was overstated and job-losses were offset by higher spending and economic activity.

Recent studies, such as evaluations of sharp minimum wage increases in places like Seattle, show that high-wage floors can slow down the hiring of low-wage workers and reduce total work hours rather than cause immediate mass layoffs.
To offset higher baseline pay, employers often resort to unpredictable scheduling, fewer workplace perks, or higher output demands that can lead to increased workplace accidents.
High minimum wages are a blunt tool for fighting poverty because many minimum-wage earners live in households with high-earning family members.
Businesses, especially in labour-intensive or low-margin sectors, frequently pass higher wage costs onto consumers through rising prices, triggering affordability pressures.

The Economist highlights alternatives such as in-work tax credits, the progressive wage policy (PWP) in Malaysia or reverse income taxes, as superior approaches because they target low-income households directly without creating the same economic distortions or hidden costs.
Regular readers of this column will be familiar with these ideas because I have advocated them for many years and they have recently been adopted by Bersama.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
64567d3842b124bd: PARIS: A French Mirage 2000D fighter jet crashed in northeastern France during a training flight, killing both crew members, officials said on Wednesday.
The plane went down at 2100 GMT on Tuesday near its air base on the outskirts of the city of Nancy.
During a press briefing in Doha, where he is on a visit, President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday expressed "the nation's condolences".
Neither the pilot, aged 27, nor his 44-year-old navigator had time to eject before the aircraft hit the ground, Metz prosecutor David Touvet told AFP on Wednesday evening.
The motors from the ejection seats were found at the crash site.
"Given the violence of the impact, no element of the investigation allows us to think that either of the two crew members will be found alive," Touvet said.
DNA analyses, which could take several weeks, will have to be carried out to identify the victims, he said.

The crew comprised "a highly experienced navigator and a young pilot who arrived at the base with all the prerequisites and qualifications needed to fly" a Mirage, air base commander Ludovic Humbert said.
"The pilot had 450 flight hours," Colonel David Pappalardo, spokesman for the Air and Space Force (AAE), told reporters in Paris.
He was "in the process of qualifying as an operational combat pilot", he said.

"At the end of the tactical phase of the training exercise, during the return at night, flying on instruments, air traffic control lost radio and radar contact," Pappalardo said, adding that there was no distress signal and "no attempt to eject".

"With my husband, we felt the walls of our house shake a little before 11pm. We heard a kind of loud bang, like when an aircraft breaks the sound barrier, but worse," nearby resident Sandra Rotatinti told AFP.
Although they saw nothing, their neighbour, who was out walking his dog at the time, saw "a ball of fire in the sky" and called the fire brigade.
The plane crashed in a wooded area.
The two-seat Mirage 2000D fighter jet entered service in 1993. France has used it in conflicts in Kosovo in 1999, Libya in 2011, Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria and Africa's Sahel region.

Several have been involved in accidents. In January 2019, both crew members aboard one making a low-altitude night flight died in eastern France. In July 2021, the crew of another managed to eject when their aircraft went down near Nancy.
France has just completed a renovation programme for its fleet of Mirage 2000Ds, which it intends to keep in service into the 2030s.
12e37ed2ae0946cd: WASHINGTON: Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites Wednesday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet.
PHP sits underneath popular web design platforms, so the weaknesses potentially affect a vast range of websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services.

Wiz, one of the security firms that found the flaws, estimated that PHP runs about 70% of the world's websites and said they rank "among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history."
The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline.
Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed.
Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online.
The flaws "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," the NSA said in a statement on X.
Attackers could use them to take over web servers without needing a password.

Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the PHP Foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.

The discovery came amid a surge in software security disclosures driven by increasingly powerful AI models, with the number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 on track to roughly double last year's record total.
PHP programmers released a fix on Wednesday.
"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.
Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI said on X that it considered the flaws "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory," adding that the discovery "marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact."
'Often and fast'

Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School who studies AI, said companies he talks to are struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to guard against AI-driven cyberattacks.
"Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast," he wrote on X.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP's developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Details leaked online Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them.
In France, local government websites, including one for the Paris police, were made inaccessible at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said.

In the Netherlands, the national digital identity service DigiD, the website of the House of Representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity center went offline as a precaution, according to Dutch public broadcaster NOS.
In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate said its own cyber.gov.au site was among government websites affected by the flaws, according to Australian public broadcaster ABC.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, warned users they could see outages on its sites while it addressed the flaws, and said it had deliberately taken many of its supporting services offline until they could be safely patched.

Several Pokemon apps, including Pokemon HOME, Pokemon Champions and Pokemon Sleep, also went offline Wednesday for emergency maintenance, with Pokemon Sleep citing security measures, according to gaming news site Kotaku.
The operator of the hit Japanese game Umamusume said it was carrying out maintenance to fix a PHP vulnerability found in its servers.

ff4b93c0a1e7a6f2: NEW YORK: US e-commerce platform eBay will cut some 1,000 jobs, or about nine percent of its workforce, a spokesman told AFP on Wednesday, following an initial round of layoffs in February.
The company informed staff of the cuts on Tuesday, according to a statement from the spokesman.

The step was taken "to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesman said, adding that eBay is "committed to supporting them through this transition with care and respect."
eBay had 12,300 employees at the end of 2025, before announcing a first round of layoffs in February affecting 800 jobs.
When presenting first- and second-quarter results earlier this year, executives at the San Jose, California-based company made no mention of the job cuts.
After several difficult years marked by near-stagnant revenue, eBay returned to growth in 2025 and saw an acceleration in the first half of this year.
In July, the group took control of clothing resale site Depop for US$1.2 billion, seeking to capitalise on the rise of the secondhand apparel market.
In early May, video game retailer GameStop made an unsolicited takeover offer valuing eBay at US$55.5 billion.
GameStop chief Ryan Cohen argued that the group was poorly managed and not innovative enough.
The board ultimately rejected the offer, with investors questioning how the deal would be financed.

15a5d78b4250b962: KUALA LUMPUR: Pearly Tan-M. Thinaah picked up where they left off in Denmark as they cruised into the French Open second round on Wednesday, setting up an all-Malaysian showdown with Ong Xin Yee-Carmen Ting.

1a1cd4631c96d2ec: LAGOS: The Ebola case detected in Nigeria is the Bundibugyo strain behind a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), officials said on Wednesday, marking the spread of the deadly disease to more parts of Africa.

The case, detected in a woman diplomat in Nigeria — the first there since the current outbreak in the DRC — has revived memories of a widespread outbreak in 2014 that struck several countries in the region.
Nigeria is the fourth African country affected by the outbreak, which this week spread across the continent, with Kenya in the east reporting nine cases since Oct 6.
The DRC's Ebola epidemic has become the deadliest in the country's history, killing 4,381 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since mid-May, according to health authorities.
The patient in Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, travelled from Uganda to the capital, Abuja, on Oct 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said.
"We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo," said Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the NCDC.
The World Health Organization (WHO) also confirmed that it was the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment.
"This person is actually a diplomat," another official said, adding that the patient's condition had deteriorated to "multi-organ failure". The official did not disclose the diplomat's nationality.
In August, Uganda was officially declared Ebola-free by the WHO after recording 20 cases — almost all of them in people who had travelled from the DRC.

Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) director-general Jean Kaseya warned on Tuesday of "an extremely serious threat", with fatality rates in the DRC rapidly approaching 50 per cent.

The Africa CDC has called a high-level meeting of health ministers for next Wednesday to assess the outbreak, coordinate cross-border efforts, support affected countries and strengthen continental preparedness.
'Geographically widespread'

"This Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has already become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history, affecting multiple countries across three regions of Africa," Kaseya said, calling for urgent international action.
Nigeria has identified 44 contacts who are being monitored, while intensifying efforts to find others who may have been exposed.
The WHO said in a statement that infection prevention and control measures were being "ramped up" at the private hospital where the patient sought care.
Nigeria's successful containment of an Ebola outbreak in 2014 has raised confidence that the country can respond effectively to new public health threats.
That epidemic killed more than 11,000 people across West Africa between late 2013 and 2016.

In an interview with AFP, former NCDC director Abdulsalami Nasidi expressed confidence that Nigeria could contain the outbreak as it did 12 years ago, but said success would depend on funding and commitment from the presidency.
"Nigeria was able to rapidly control 2014 Ebola outbreak because they took the right actions at the right time, had good command structures on the ground," Nasidi said.
The response to the latest outbreak could test President Bola Tinubu's re-election bid as Nigeria prepares for presidential polls in January.
In a statement on Wednesday by Tinubu's media adviser, Bayo Onanuga, a presidential task force on Ebola said it was confident Nigeria would be "able to dent this outbreak".
2014 outbreak
In 2014, the first Nigerian case, detected in Lagos, the country's commercial hub of more than 20 million people, raised fears that the highly contagious virus would spread rapidly.
However, a swift response by Nigerian authorities, supported by international organisations, helped bring the epidemic under control within 21 days, resulting in only 19 infections and seven deaths.
"It was so shocking when we got the news yesterday," Anthony Ojogho, a 42-year-old civil servant, told AFP on the streets of Abuja on Wednesday morning.
But he was confident in the authorities' ability to contain the spread of the virus, citing Nigeria's previous experience.
Governments "have always been equal to the task. We contained Ebola, we contained coronavirus," he said.
"If the right steps are being taken, I'm very sure that we're going to contain to a large extent the spread of Ebola virus in Nigeria."

0dfe6a4ce53e853e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — If you are given a pot of money, would you spend it all in one go or over just a few years, or would you make it last for the rest of your life?
Shifting away from lump-sum EPF withdrawals towards lifelong income

At the recent Employees Provident Fund (EPF) International Social Wellbeing Conference 2026 (ISWC 2026), global pension expert William Price said the idea of accessing retirement savings as a lump sum is deeply embedded in Malaysian society, partly because of expectations or plans to help one's children pay for their education, a house or a wedding, for example.

Price said, however, that viewing retirement savings as a “pot of assets” could almost blind people into thinking they have a lot of money, while focusing on it as “income” would provide a “reality check”.

While people tend to have more savings and a greater ability to work or remain active in the early years of retirement, he noted that OECD data showed older people (aged 76 and above) were poorer on average in virtually all OECD countries.
In an interview with Malay Mail, Price proposed three possible solutions for Malaysia:
1. Introduce a non-contributory pension, raise the retirement age and increase the EPF withdrawal age
(If there is an integrated reform of both private and public pensions)

Unlike a defined-contribution retirement savings scheme such as the EPF, where members contribute to their own retirement savings, a non-contributory pension provides retirement benefits without requiring recipients to have made contributions.
Price said non-contributory pensions had been fundamental to reducing old-age poverty in other countries, noting that some people were unpaid carers or unable to work.

“And you just have to accept there will be some people, in the way that some people never work; some people are disabled; some people are lifetime poor; some people were working non-stop, but just not paid because they were caring or whatever the circumstances were,” he said at ISWC 2026.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

William Price, a former global pension expert with the World Bank who has also worked with the UK Treasury and UK Pensions Regulator, said Malaysia could raise its retirement age and EPF withdrawal age while introducing a tax-funded pension from age 75. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin

Price proposed that the government introduce a tax-funded “non-contributory pension” for all Malaysians aged 75 and above, providing a minimum income sufficient to cover basic living expenses, such as groceries.

“So if there was an integrated reform, what I would do is that there would be a non-contributory pension for everyone at 75,” he told Malay Mail, adding that it could be taxable for wealthy recipients or tax-free for those relying on it as their sole source of income.
Why 75? Price said introducing non-contributory pensions from that age would be more affordable, as the population aged 75 and above is relatively smaller than those aged 60 or 65 and above.
Currently, Malaysia's minimum retirement age is 60, while Malaysians can choose to withdraw their entire EPF savings or make monthly or partial withdrawals from as early as age 55.

Alongside the proposed government-funded pension kicking in at 75, he also suggested raising both the retirement age and the age at which members can access their EPF savings as a lump sum to 60 or 65.
This would help people preserve their savings for longer and ensure they have sufficient income until at least age 75.

“So you say to people, ‘your money has to last until 75 at least’. And so they’ve got a kind of a fixed window of time. They’re like ‘okay, so I need to save enough to mean that I’ve got enough until I’m aged 75, and then the government will give me ‘X’,” the CEO of pension consultancy firm D3P Global told Malay Mail.

Those who feel the proposed non-contributory pension would be insufficient to meet their needs after age 75 could plan to retain some of their EPF savings beyond that age, allowing them to rely on a combination of both income sources in later life.
2. Set aside some EPF savings to generate income from age 75 onwards
(If there is no integrated reform of the public and private pension systems)
In a scenario where the government does not introduce a non-contributory pension, Price proposed that Malaysians set aside part of their EPF savings to provide an income after turning 75.

In his ISWC presentation, Price illustrated how a retiree could make withdrawals from their pension savings over a 10-year period (say, from age 65 to 75), while a portion of their retirement balance is used each year to fund a “deferred annuity” that would provide income for the rest of their life after turning 75.
Noting that the actual method would depend on what people find acceptable, Price outlined to Malay Mail several possible options:
Set a minimum level of EPF savings that everyone must have by age 75, with part of their EPF savings transferred to a fund for those aged 75 and above (75+ fund) from age 60 or 65 onwards.
Savings not transferred to the 75+ fund could still be accessed before age 75.
Savings transferred to the fund could only be accessed after age 75, but would go to beneficiaries if the member dies before reaching that age.
Begin transferring savings to the 75+ fund at an earlier age, such as 35, 40 or 45.
Transfer only the annual EPF dividends, for example, from age 55 or 60 onwards, to the 75+ fund.
Price explained that there was nothing “magic” about the number 75 and that the proposal could also be used to ensure an income from other ages, such as 70.

“So, the number kind of depends on the population and the amount of savings they have. But because lots of people don't have a lot of EPF savings, you can't really afford to have a guaranteed minimum from age 60 until you die. It's just too expensive,” he told Malay Mail.
As for the EPF withdrawal age, he said it could be raised gradually, first from 55 to 60 and eventually to 65.<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A variable annuity could help ensure retirees continue receiving an income throughout their lives. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
3. Introduce a variable annuity designed to provide income for life
Price said the EPF currently pools or shares investment risk among its members, but does not pool longevity risk.
In other words, members face the risk of living longer than their EPF savings can last.
He proposed that the EPF introduce a variable annuity, under which members would share both investment and longevity risks.
Under this proposal, members would have access to only a portion of their EPF savings, such as 10 per cent or 25 per cent, while the EPF would invest the remainder to generate lifelong income.

“The majority of your EPF money is invested. And from the age of 60 or 65, you are paid an income which will last until you die, and the amount of that income will depend on the balances that you have, the amount of savings you have,” he said, adding that the EPF could continue managing the investments as it currently does.
Explaining the pooling of mortality or longevity risk, Price said no one could predict how long they would live.

“So the people who die young get less; the people who die much later, they still get the income until they die. So you don't have to deal with the risk that you may live too long and outlive your savings,” he told Malay Mail.
He said income from the variable annuity could be taxable or tax-free, depending on the recipient's wealth.
Typically, with insured fixed annuities, insurance companies assume the longevity risk and guarantee a fixed annual payment until a person's death in exchange for a lump-sum payment.
Under Price's proposal, however, the annual income paid through a variable annuity would not be fixed but would depend on both investment performance and how long people in the pool live.
“If everyone is living longer than we expected, your annual payments will be a bit lower,” he said, adding that the lifelong payouts could be recalculated annually or based on an average.
Price said Malaysia could adopt any of the “three basic ideas” he had proposed as solutions.
“And it just depends which is the most politically acceptable and achievable.”

5f4feba4a3339b96: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Licensed financial planner Rajen Devadason said an insurance annuity scheme like Singapore’s CPF LIFE could also work in Malaysia.
He explained that if the government gives a long runway, and make it politically more palatable by using automatic enrolment and giving people a chance to opt out, a similar scheme may be acceptable.
He was speaking to Malay Mail at the sidelines of the recent Employees Provident Fund’s (EPF) International Social Wellbeing Conference 2026 (ISWC 2026).

Rajen said there might be the risk of a political backlash if access or withdrawals from EPF savings at ages 50, 55 and 60 is changed so one possibility is to keep the same withdrawal rules while using a small portion of EPF savings for an annuity.
“But if let’s say you increase your retirement age to 65 and you don’t change the withdrawal parameters at 50, 55, and 60, people are cool, no problems.
“But if you then give people the opportunity to work longer, that funding between 60 and 65, if all of that flowed into an annuity, that might work, might help,” he added.
Rajen believes something like an annuity insurance would be a “step in the right direction” for Malaysia, based on global experience.
“But by itself, it’s not enough. People must take personal responsibility. They have to build their own private pensions,” he said, adding that this should run in parallel with working longer.

“The whole purpose of working longer is that you can build a higher pile of retirement savings,” he said, also saying these funds should be used as capital to create multiple streams of passive income for retirement.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
ILO senior social protection specialist Mariko Ouchi said different countries have different problems which means they would need their own pension solutions. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
No ‘one size fits all’ when designing retirement or pension systems
International Labour Organisation’s (ILO) senior social protection specialist for South Asia Mariko Ouchi said there is no “one perfect model” or “one fit for all” pension model in the world.

“Many people ask me what is the best model or good practice in terms of pension and old-age benefit in the world. And then I answer, all countries are having problems in one way or another. So, there is no ‘one perfect model’ as such,” she said in her presentation at the ISWC 2026.
She said each country will have to find solutions best suited to their different circumstances: “Malaysia has to seek its own solution to provide the best income guarantee for the elderly people.”

Ouchi said countries go through many changes, such as the different work nature including international jobs done remotely; migration; demography; higher life expectancies; higher retirement ages; and higher pension access ages.

She added it is important for countries to carry out periodic reviews or periodic actuarial evaluation on a country’s old-age benefit model (such as every three years or every five years) depending on the country and its system’s stability.

Countries also need to carry out a mid-term to long-term revisiting of their existing pension models, to see if it could continue running for decades unchanged or if substantial reforms are needed, Ouchi explained.

aec603cefb8de3dd: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Singapore’s Central Provident Fund Board (CPFB) deputy CEO (services) Wong Yan Jun said Singapore’s CPF — the equivalent of Malaysia’s EPF — had in 1987 introduced a phased withdrawal scheme.
The Retirement Sum Scheme (RSS) splits up monthly payouts of a Singaporean’s retirement savings over a fixed duration of 20 years to make it last longer.
This was because the government realised the lump sum withdrawal option at age 55 was less suited to support retirement over many years, as Singaporeans were living longer.

Singapore in 2007 recognised that more than half of Singaporean men and women would live past 82 and 85 respectively, which led to the 2009 introduction of the national longevity insurance annuity scheme, “CPF Lifelong Income for the Elderly” (CPF LIFE).
Back in 2007, many Singaporeans wrote to CPFB to challenge the idea that half of Singaporeans would live past 85, pointing out that most obituaries then showed people dying at ages like 75 and 80.
“But the truth is what we are preparing for is not for that moment. CPF LIFE is preparing for the future generation to come,” he said, adding that Singapore ultimately managed to push it through.
He said CPF LIFE pools the longevity risk to give Singaporeans the confidence that they can have income for as long as they live.

When asked at the Employees Provident Fund’s (EPF) International Social Wellbeing Conference 2026 (ISWC 2026) panel session if CPF LIFE would need government subsidies to sustain lifetime payouts, he said the scheme is fully self-sustainable as the entire CPF LIFE funds are invested in Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS) with a guaranteed risk-free return of about four per cent.

He also said CPF LIFE has very low expenses as compared to annuities provided by the private sector, as CPFB is a non-profit organisation and does not have intermediary fees such as agents’ commissions.

He said CPF LIFE’s monthly payouts are not a guaranteed or fixed number, which provides flexibility to adjust monthly payouts if necessary to ensure that the scheme can continue to be self-sustaining.
According to CPFB’s website, CPF members can join CPF LIFE anytime from age 65 and up to one month before turning 80.

CPF LIFE automatically includes those born after 1958 and with a minimum S$60,000 in CPF retirement savings by age 65, with Wong telling Malay Mail that nine in 10 CPF members are expected to reach this savings level by 2035.
Wong said those who do not meet the minimum S$60,000 level would be on the RSS plan (where payouts are only while savings last), but noted they can still opt in for CPF Life.
Those automatically included under CPF Life cannot be exempted from it, unless they have a pension or commercial annuity that gives the same or higher monthly payouts.

4bfe4e6d7d791ebe: NEW YORK, Oct 22 — US aviation giant Boeing’s commercial plane fleet is composed of four different aircraft families. The company had 6,863 plane orders at the end of September.
The 737 MAX, the most popular
The single-aisle jet, first launched in August 2011, emits fewer greenhouse gas emissions than earlier aircraft and is designed to be half as noisy.
Boeing has sold more 737 planes than any other family, but the aircraft was dethroned by Airbus’ A320 as the most-sold plane in October 2025.
There are four versions of the MAX, ranging from the smallest, the 737 MAX 7, to the largest — the 737 MAX 10. US authorities certified both models in 2026.
The MAX 7 can fly up to 7,040 kilometers (4,400 miles) while the MAX 10 can fly up to 5,740 kilometers (3,600 miles). Both are expected to enter airline fleets in 2027.
The other two models are currently in use. The 737 MAX 8 was responsible for two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019 in which 346 people died.
According to aviation publication Leeham News, Boeing amassed nearly $44 billion in special charges between 2018 and 2025 for all commercial jets, with the MAX responsible for around half.
The 787 Dreamliner
First coming into use in 2011, this type of plane has transported some 1.3 billion passengers.
The plane, known for greater fuel efficiency than earlier models, is the fastest-selling wide-body aircraft in aviation history.
Boeing says the aircraft’s onboard systems monitor the operational state of the vessel, signaling if maintenance is needed.
There are three versions of the plane, carrying between 200 and 375 passengers. They can fly to peak distances of between 13,890 kilometers (8,600 miles) and 15,370 kilometers (9,550 miles).
Since 2021, Boeing consolidated production of the jet to South Carolina, where the company is adding a second assembly line.
The 777X, the newest
Boeing has faced numerous delays on the 777X, the latest generation of the long-range, 777 aircraft, the most-built wide-body aircraft.
Boeing unveiled the most recent incarnation of the jet, the 777X, in 2013.

Deliveries were originally targeted for 2020, but the company has hit numerous obstacles during the certification process. The company is now targeting 2027 deliveries, but the aircraft is still not certified.
There are three versions, seating between 350 and 450 people. Maximum distances ranges from 14,820 kilometers (9,200 miles) to 17,590 kilometers (10,900 miles).
The 777-8 is considered a direct rival of the Airbus A350-1000.
The 767 family
First certified in the 1980s, this aircraft has a long history of flying transcontinental routes. Boeing still builds new 767 jets for cargo work and in a military version known as the KC-46. — AFP
bf364b3ed14e478b: WASHINGTON, Oct 22 — For years, Max Salas has enjoyed teeing off at Washington’s East Potomac Golf Links, a public course nestled in the heart of the US capital where ordinary Americans can enjoy a round without breaking the bank.
But President Donald Trump’s controversial plans to remodel the course into a facility capable of hosting major championship- caliber events have left the 74-year-old retiree exasperated.
“Leave us alone! Leave us alone!” Salas told AFP when asked what message he would send to Trump.
“What the hell do we need a championship course in a public course?” he said. “We’re here, we’ve been here for years, and it’s ridiculous.”
Salas is among golfers worried that Trump’s proposed overhaul of East Potomac could transform an affordable public amenity into an expensive destination beyond the reach of its regular players.
At the moment, 18 holes at East Potomac costs a maximum of US$48 (RM195).
That’s a far cry from the kind of rates often found at privately owned golf courses — such as those owned by Trump — where green fees can often run into hundreds of dollars.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A golfer plays on the course near cut down trees at East Potomac Golf Links near Hains Point in Washington, DC, October 19, 2026. — AFP
Trump, a famously avid golfer, has claimed that East Potomac is not fit for purpose.
“The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect,” Trump said on Sunday.
“It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall.”
But for Salas, the remodel — which will see the course closed from mid-November — also raises questions about Trump’s priorities at a time of international turmoil.
“We’re in the middle of a war, and he’s over here trying to tinker with a golf course?” he said. “I mean, where is this guy’s sense? Common sense?”
‘I cannot afford it’
The prospect of a championship-standard course might appeal to some golfers, but for others, the overriding concern is what the transformation could mean for their wallets.
Fidel Enrique Garcia Rendon, a 59-year-old Pilates studio owner, fears the cost of playing the remodeled course will put it beyond his reach.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A golfer plays on the course at East Potomac Golf Links near Hains Point in Washington, DC, October 19, 2026. US President Donald Trump on October 18, 2026, unveiled his plans for overhauling a beloved municipal golf course in the US capital, a project already mired in a contentious legal fight. — AFP pic
“Unfortunately, if it goes to a championship course level, the fees are going to go from US$22 to US$250 or plus, US$350 who knows?” he said.
“So I definitely will not be able to come here and play because at that price, I cannot afford it.”
His concerns were echoed by fellow retiree Tom Carmody, who questioned both the eventual cost of the revamped course and whether the project would be completed.
“It just makes me nervous, quite nervous,” Carmody said.
“For one, just his ability to follow through. I mean, what’s going to happen? Will he stop halfway through or quit or something like that?”
But Carmody’s bigger concern is whether the promise of continued public access will mean much if green fees rise dramatically.
“He talks about it remaining open to the public, but instead of US$30 or US$40 a round, maybe it’s US$120, US$150 a round, which is going to eliminate a lot of people.” — AFP
7b3ed723bff94bce: KYIV, Oct 22 — The air alert ends at 8.15am with an explosion in the distance, allowing Anastasiia Zhmutska to finally take her 14-year-old son Orest to school in Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv.

Anastasiia, 44, is a busy mother with three children, a job at a hospital and little time for herself. Since the end of summer, Russia has “added a few extra tasks”, she said with a mischievous glint that barely conceals her fatigue.
Air raid alerts and explosions shatter her nights and set the rhythm of her days, as Russia steps up drone attacks that have killed more than 190 people in Kyiv since January.
Whether it’s the school run or keeping an eye on Orest’s 19-year-old brother, her timetable is organised depending on the risk of strikes.
The previous evening, she took her five-year-old daughter to safety at a second home with her father, far away from the attacks.
At school, she looks into her bag containing two battery power packs that she will recharge at work, where the electricity supply is uninterrupted.
After supermarkets and petrol stations, Russia is again attacking the power network, which has led to outages.
“It’s becoming more complicated,” Anastasiia told AFP. “But it still has to be dealt with.”
When the power comes back on in her flat, she quickly runs to put on a load of washing. For everything else, she uses a string of Christmas lights for illumination.
“There’s always a way out of any everyday situation,” she added. “At the very least, I’ve managed to find a way out over the past five years.”
Sleepless nights
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Anastasiia Zhmutska, 44 years old, stands in a bus on her way home after work, in Kyiv on October 13, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. — AFP pic
Anastasiia drops Orest at school with a peck on the cheek and heads to the hospital. Orest lowers his gaze under a lock of blond hair as he settles at his desk — alone.
The classroom gradually fills with a succession of tired faces after another sleepless night.
Literature teacher Nadia Sherekhor admitted that Russian attacks have affected the quality of lessons. “Kyiv doesn’t sleep,” she said.
At 9 am, a minute’s silence is held in memory of those who have died since 2022. The children stand with their hands on their hearts as the Ukrainian national anthem plays over loudspeakers.
The lesson resumed. Stretching sessions help the children cope with anxiety.
At 10.44am, Russian drones were detected approaching Kyiv and the air raid alarm sounded.
Laughing and shouting, the children crossed the courtyard and disappeared into an underground space beneath the school.
Everyone finds a corner of a table for their English and maths exercise books in the cramped corridor.
Orest is used to bomb shelters and explosions but in recent months he has become more anxious. “I keep everything to myself,” he said.
Above ground, a drone screamed over the school, anti-aircraft fire crackled and a man looked up at the skies. The drone disappeared and a detonation echoed in the distance.
Breaking point
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Orest and his classmates head down to the shelter during an air alert in Kyiv on October 13, 2026. — AFP pic
At the hospital, Anastasiia chatted with her colleagues about which canned goods to buy and how much water to stockpile.
“I’m always thinking about how to organise myself because for me the hardest part is making decisions,” she said. “I carry this burden of responsibility all the time.”
Anastasiia keeps an eye on her telephone, switching between school WhatsApp groups, Telegram channels monitoring Russian drones and Orest’s GPS tracker.
At 2pm, the teenager left school for gymnastics training before the power cuts paralyse public transport. He dreams of becoming an Olympic athlete.
“Before I answer him, I’ve already monitored everything: I’ve looked to see whether the route has changed, whether the metro has been shut down,” his mother said.
Anastasiia’s heightened state of alertness went to another level on October 14 when a Russian drone hit a business centre between her school and home.
A student who was waiting for his bus was severely wounded.
Fragments from the explosion fell onto Anastasiia’s apartment building.
At 6pm, she is on the bus and the family is heading to their second home on the other side of the Dnipro river that cuts through Kyiv.
“It’s a peaceful place,” she said. “But getting there is an ordeal.”
Traffic jams build up at the approach to the Southern Bridge, which has been closed since Russian drones slammed into it the previous week.
At rush hour, the traffic is chaotic and it takes Anastasiia two hours to travel 15 kilometres (nearly 10 miles).
“It feels like it can’t get any harder than it is right now but I know it will,” she said.
She sent a last message before her phone switched off, asking her daughter to wait for her before she goes to sleep. A promised treat is in her bag.
Asked what would be the breaking point that would make her leave Kyiv, Anastasiia went quiet for several seconds.
“I’ve already asked myself this question several times,” she said finally. “And I don’t know the answer.” — AFP
0b2a48db9204741f: PARIS: Police banned protests in parts of Paris on Thursday as France braced for more demonstrations, just days after student and other rallies degenerated into some of the worst street unrest in years.

The announcement on Wednesday came after President Emmanuel Macron took an apparent swipe at his US counterpart Donald Trump for exploiting the riots for political advantage in the US midterm election campaign.

The Paris ban will last from 8am to 8pm (0600 to 1800 GMT) and apply to key landmarks in the French capital, including the Elysee presidential palace, both houses of parliament, as well as tourist attractions such as the Louvre museum and the Champs-Elysees.
Other areas where rallies will be prohibited include Bastille and Republique squares, and the Chatelet-Les Halles shopping area, which was heavily targeted by looters over the weekend.
France has admitted it "lost control" amid the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised public buildings.

As his government struggled to contain a crisis that has damaged France's image abroad and rattled financial markets six months before presidential elections, Macron implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also fighting an election campaign, had made "stupid comments" on the unrest for political gain.
"There are people who campaign at France's expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," he told reporters in Doha.
Trump has sought to link the unrest to "migrants, jihadists, and communists" as he campaigned for his Republican Party in the US with an anti-immigration message.
He also praised French far-right leader Marine Le Pen on Tuesday. She shares his ideologies.
Le Pen late on Wednesday branded Macron's remarks as "conspiratorial" in a post on X.

"The images we saw last Saturday are not generated by artificial intelligence: they show the sad reality of what France has become after 10 years of Macronist rule," added the far-right candidate, who is leading in the polls for the 2027 presidential election.
Several analysts have dismissed claims that migrants were driving France's protests.
'New phase' upcoming

The unrest overshadowed demonstrations on Saturday, when more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France.
Following the rioting — the worst France has seen in years — and ahead of fresh cost-of-living demonstrations planned for Saturday, Macron's government has warned it will brook no further violence.
Fresh demonstrations planned by high school pupils and university students were similarly banned in both Paris and the southeastern city of Lyon.
Following a meeting with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Wednesday, the leader of France's hardline CGT union, Sophie Binet, called for a "new phase" of protests, with strikes early next month.

ddbc280478901f4d: Peter Steinberger, member of technical staff at OpenAI and the creator of OpenClaw, estimates that he spent around $10 million in tokens running AI workloads last month. But don't feel bad for him, because it's all coming out of investors' pockets.

"I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?"

Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally?

Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI.
Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code.
"If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said.
Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years.
Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds.

"I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer."
Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent.

That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model.
"A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said.
Even if risks like prompt injection have been reduced through engineering efforts, Steinberger said, "you might not want to give your agent all the permissions."
Instead, he suggested using an agent to authorize your agent.

"You want to have another agent that can give it permissions or not and then this agent has to negotiate with another agent," he said. "Many times the agents are like, 'oh yeah, actually maybe I shouldn't do this,' or 'there's a simpler way that keeps it within the guardrails.' c91866ae59011088: Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable, a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices.

If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone.
You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy. Lame.

Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves.

As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it.

The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised).
Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved.

Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands.

In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of 2 minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper.
Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use.

A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening the clock app and switching to the stopwatch tab takes it about 96 seconds, which is supposed to be impressive, apparently, as the company behind Opposable decided to showcase it on the thing’s website.
As for Opposable’s ability to actually accomplish tasks, well, that’s not exactly a sure thing.

“On eight tasks the model had never been tuned on, run on the emulator twice each, giving it the whole task succeeded 4 and 3 times,” the blog post notes. I’m pretty sure my brain and hands can do better without burning tokens to fail.

“Giving it one subgoal at a time and checking each claimed success against the accessibility tree before the next subgoal succeeded 6 times in both rounds,” the blog continues - so even when it gets babysat each step of the way, it still only succeeds at three-quarters of tasks. Cool - that’s really going to free up all that time wasted setting timers and doing other mundane tasks on my handset.

Why someone would install this on their Android device - which requires sideloading an APK and manually granting access to read and interact with the screen through accessibility settings - seems like a bit of a mystery. Opposable’s website even warns that it could be a security disaster: “whoever holds the token can operate the phone, so treat it like a password,” but still invites users to try.

An argument could be made for using Opposable as an accessibility tool for people with difficulty using a smartphone, but this isn’t mentioned anywhere on its website. Opposable is instead billed as a way to “hand off the phone chores,” leaving users free to do something else - just not on the phone currently being slowly controlled by a clumsy AI.
Sure, you could give your AI some virtual thumbs through Opposable, but … why? We reached out to the Opposable team to get an answer to that question, but didn’t hear back. ®
